fuentes/capitulaciones-de-santa-fe/sopor.texto: Capitulation signed by Ferdinand and Isabella on April 17, 1492, drafted by the secretary Juan de Coloma

fuentes/capitulaciones-de-santa-fe/resum.texto: Contract between the Catholic Monarchs and Christopher Columbus before the first voyage. For the islands and mainlands he “discovers or wins,” it grants him the titles of admiral, viceroy and governor, with the admiralty made hereditary, and a tenth of the merchandise and metals obtained there. The title of Granada of April 30 completed the privileges.

fuentes/capitulaciones-de-santa-fe/por_q.texto: It is the legal origin of the Columbus family's government in Hispaniola and of the Columbian lawsuits, in which the Crown spent decades cutting back those privileges for the admiral's heirs.

fuentes/diario-de-colon/titulo.texto: Diary of Columbus's first voyage (summary by Bartolomé de las Casas)

fuentes/diario-de-colon/soporte.texto: Handwritten summary by Las Casas, c. 1530; the original and the copy delivered to the monarchs were lost

fuentes/diario-de-colon/resumen.texto: A day-by-day account of the 1492–1493 voyage, known only through Las Casas's summary, which quotes some passages verbatim and summarizes others. It describes the arrival at Guanahaní on October 12, the route through the Bahamas, Cuba and Hispaniola, the Lucayans and Taínos as a peaceful and unarmed people who “must make good servants,” the constant search for gold, and the first news of the “caniba” who ate men. It recounts the wreck of the Santa María and the founding of La Navidad. It also notes that he had several Indians seized to take to Castile and that with fifty men they could be kept subjugated.

fuentes/diario-de-colon/por_que_importa.texto: It is the most direct document of the first encounter, but it reaches us filtered through Las Casas, who summarized it decades later. Part of the scholarship debates which phrases are Columbus's and which belong to the summary.

fuentes/diario-de-colon/leer.0.titulo.texto: Text of the Las Casas summary at Wikisource

fuentes/diario-de-colon/leer.1.titulo.texto: English translation by Clements Markham (Hakluyt Society, 1893), at Internet Archive

fuentes/carta-de-colon-1493/titulo.texto: Columbus's letter announcing the discovery (letter to Luis de Santángel)

fuentes/carta-de-colon-1493/soporte.texto: Dated February 15, 1493, on the return voyage; printed in Barcelona in April 1493 and in Latin in Rome that same year

fuentes/carta-de-colon-1493/resumen.texto: Letter in which Columbus announces that he has reached “the Indies” and taken possession of many islands. He describes the inhabitants as naked people without iron weapons, “timid” and generous, without “sect or idolatry.” He speaks of gold, spices and cotton, and mentions an island inhabited by people “who eat human flesh” and another of women alone. He promises the monarchs gold and slaves, “as many as they order to be loaded.”

fuentes/carta-de-colon-1493/por_que_impo.texto: It was the first printed text about America and circulated throughout Europe in 1493–1494. From the start it set the division between tame Indians and cannibals, which later had legal consequences.

fuentes/carta-de-colon-1493/leer.0.titul.texto: Facsimile and transcription of the Barcelona edition of 1493 (London, 1893), at Internet Archive

fuentes/carta-de-colon-1493/leer.1.titul.texto: Castilian text with English translation in Select Letters of Christopher Columbus (Hakluyt Society, 1870), at Internet Archive

fuentes/carta-de-chanca/titulo.texto: Letter from Dr. Chanca to the cabildo of Seville

fuentes/carta-de-chanca/soporte.texto: Preserved in a later copy; published by Martín Fernández de Navarrete in 1825

fuentes/carta-de-chanca/resumen.texto: Account by the physician of the second voyage's fleet of the crossing, the Lesser Antilles, the arrival in Hispaniola and the founding of La Isabela. He describes the abandoned villages of Guadeloupe, with human bones and Taíno women captives whom, he says, the Caribs took as women, and boys they captured and castrated in order to eat them. He says that in one house they found a man's neck cooking in a pot. He also recounts the discovery of La Navidad destroyed and the diseases of the colonists.

fuentes/carta-de-chanca/por_que_importa.texto: Together with Cuneo's, it is the main source on Carib cannibalism, written by a witness to the villages but not to the acts, and the first medical and natural description written in America.

fuentes/carta-de-chanca/leer.0.titulo.texto: Castilian text with English translation in Select Letters of Christopher Columbus (Hakluyt Society, 1870), at Internet Archive

fuentes/carta-de-michele-da-cuneo/titulo.texto: Letter from Michele da Cuneo to Gerolamo Annari

fuentes/carta-de-michele-da-cuneo/soport.texto: Manuscript in the University Library of Bologna, published in the late 19th century

fuentes/carta-de-michele-da-cuneo/resume.texto: Letter from a companion of Columbus on the second voyage. It recounts the capture of Caribs in the Lesser Antilles and that he himself raped a captive woman whom Columbus had given him. It describes life in La Isabela, the search for gold and the shipment of some 550 Taíno captives to Castile in February 1495, of whom, he says, about 200 died during the voyage and were thrown into the sea. It also repeats that the Caribs ate their captives.

fuentes/carta-de-michele-da-cuneo/por_qu.texto: It is a private letter, not written to ask for favors or to defend a cause, and that is why it is read as direct testimony to the violence of the early years and to the beginning of the trade in Indians to Castile.

fuentes/relacion-de-ramon-pane/titulo.texto: Account of the Antiquities of the Indians

fuentes/relacion-de-ramon-pane/soporte.texto: The original was lost; it survives in the Italian translation included in The Life of the Admiral Christopher Columbus by Hernando Colón (Venice, 1571), and in summaries by Peter Martyr and Las Casas

fuentes/relacion-de-ramon-pane/resumen.texto: Written at Columbus's request after about four years living among the Taínos. It gathers their accounts of the origin of humans in caves, the flood, the cemíes (idols and spirits), the behíques (healers) and the cohoba rite with hallucinogenic powders. It recounts the first conversions and that Bartholomew Columbus had some Indians burned alive who had buried and urinated on Christian images.

fuentes/relacion-de-ramon-pane/por_que_i.texto: It is the only source on Taíno religion written from within a community, and it is considered the first ethnography of the Americas.

fuentes/carta-de-colon-desde-jamaica/tit.texto: Letter from Columbus to the monarchs from Jamaica (Lettera rarissima)

fuentes/carta-de-colon-desde-jamaica/sop.texto: Dated July 7, 1503, in Jamaica; printed in Italian in Venice in 1505

fuentes/carta-de-colon-desde-jamaica/res.texto: Letter written during the fourth voyage, when Columbus was stranded in Jamaica with two unseaworthy ships. It recounts the route along the coast from Honduras to Panama, the gold of Veragua and the fights with Indigenous people. It complains of the injustices he suffered and recounts a vision in which a voice consoled him.

fuentes/carta-de-colon-desde-jamaica/por.texto: It shows Columbus at the end of his career, with his mix of exploration, interest in gold and messianism.

fuentes/carta-de-colon-desde-jamaica/lee.texto: Castilian text with English translation in Select Letters of Christopher Columbus (Hakluyt Society, 1870), at Internet Archive

fuentes/pesquisa-de-bobadilla/titulo.texto: Inquiry by Francisco de Bobadilla into the government of the Columbus family

fuentes/pesquisa-de-bobadilla/soporte.texto: Found in the Archivo General de Simancas by Isabel Aguirre and published in 2006 by Consuelo Varela

fuentes/pesquisa-de-bobadilla/resumen.texto: Testimony gathered by the inquiry judge Bobadilla about the government of Cristóbal, Bartolomé and Diego Columbus in Hispaniola. The witnesses, Spanish colonists, describe very harsh punishments of Spaniards (floggings, cut ears and noses, hangings), the hunger of the early years and the division of the gold. There are also references to the war against the Indians and to their sale as slaves.

fuentes/pesquisa-de-bobadilla/por_que_im.texto: It served to remove Columbus from office and explains why the monarchs accepted his fall. It was assembled by his rival and drawn from hostile witnesses, which must be taken into account when reading it.

fuentes/decadas-de-orbe-novo/soporte.texto: First decade printed in Seville in 1511; all eight in Alcalá in 1530

fuentes/decadas-de-orbe-novo/resumen.texto: Eight “decades” of letters and accounts in Latin that Peter Martyr wrote from the court, based on what Columbus, navigators and officials told him and on the papers that arrived. They cover from Columbus's voyages to the conquest of Mexico. They describe the nature, peoples and customs of the Antilles, record Pané's account and at times criticize the greed of the colonists.

fuentes/decadas-de-orbe-novo/por_que_imp.texto: It was the first history of America to circulate among European humanists, and it spread the expression “New World.”

fuentes/decadas-de-orbe-novo/leer.0.titu.texto: English translation by Francis MacNutt (1912), volume 1, at Project Gutenberg

fuentes/decadas-de-orbe-novo/leer.1.titu.texto: Latin edition of 1574, at Internet Archive

fuentes/sumario-de-la-natural-historia/t.texto: Summary of the Natural History of the Indies

fuentes/sumario-de-la-natural-historia/r.texto: Short book that Oviedo dedicated to Charles V, with descriptions of the plants, animals, resources and peoples of the Antilles and Tierra Firme, such as maize, cassava, the hammock, the iguana and tobacco. On Indigenous peoples it includes very negative judgments, which he later developed in his General History.

fuentes/sumario-de-la-natural-historia/p.texto: It is one of the first works of American natural history, with observations by someone who had lived for years in the Caribbean.

fuentes/historia-general-y-natural-de-la.texto: General and Natural History of the Indies
The first part was printed in Seville in 1535; the complete work only in 1851–1855

Oviedo's official chronicle, written by the chronicler of the Indies from 1532, which combines the history of the conquest, a description of nature and accounts by witnesses. On the Taínos it attributes their disappearance mainly to their vices, idolatry and suicide, though it also records the cruelty of many Spaniards. It justifies the war against rebellious Indians and the massacre of Jaragua.
It is the longest chronicle of the first decades in the Caribbean and the antagonist of Las Casas, who accused it of slandering the Indians and of defending the interests of encomenderos.
Edition by José Amador de los Ríos (Madrid, 1851), volume 1, at Internet Archive

fuentes/historia-de-las-indias-las-casas.texto: Written between 1527 and 1561; published in Madrid in 1875–1876

History of the first thirty years of the Indies, with the life of Columbus, the government of Hispaniola, the wars of Jaragua and Higüey, the conquest of Cuba (in which Las Casas took part as chaplain), Montesinos's sermon and the struggle for protective laws. It uses documents now lost, such as Columbus's diary, and his personal testimony. It accuses the colonists and Oviedo, and acknowledges his own error in proposing in 1516 the import of African slaves.

It is the richest source on Hispaniola and Cuba between 1492 and 1520, written to defend a cause. Its population figures are exaggerated, but many of the events it narrates are confirmed by other documents.
Madrid edition (1875–1876), volume 3, with the government of Ovando and the conquest of Cuba, at Internet Archive

fuentes/apologetica-historia-sumaria/sop.texto: Unpublished until the 20th century; complete edition by Edmundo O'Gorman in 1967

fuentes/apologetica-historia-sumaria/res.texto: Treatise born as part of the History of the Indies, in which Las Casas argues, using Aristotle's categories, that the peoples of the Indies had reason, government, cities and religion comparable or superior to those of the ancient Greeks and Romans. It describes the nature of Hispaniola and the customs of the Taínos, Mexica and Incas, using information from Pané, chroniclers and friars.

fuentes/apologetica-historia-sumaria/por.texto: It is Las Casas's answer to those who, like Sepúlveda and Oviedo, considered the Indians servants by nature, and one of the first works of comparative ethnology.

fuentes/apologetica-historia-sumaria/lee.texto: Edition by M. Serrano y Sanz, «Historiadores de Indias» vol. 1 (Madrid, 1909), Internet Archive

fuentes/historia-del-almirante/titulo.texto: The Life of the Admiral Christopher Columbus

fuentes/historia-del-almirante/soporte.texto: Original Castilian lost; Italian translation by Alfonso de Ulloa printed in Venice in 1571

fuentes/historia-del-almirante/resumen.texto: Life of Christopher Columbus written by his son with family papers. It narrates his four voyages and his government of Hispaniola, and defends his memory against the charges that led to his removal. It includes Ramón Pané's account, which survives only through this work.

fuentes/historia-del-almirante/por_que_i.texto: It is a central source on the voyages, written with a son's interest in the family lawsuits. In the 19th century its authenticity was debated; it is generally accepted today.

fuentes/historia-del-almirante/leer.0.ti.texto: Madrid edition (1892), volume 1, at Internet Archive

fuentes/mundus-novus/soporte.texto: Letter addressed to Lorenzo di Pierfrancesco de' Medici, printed in Latin in 1502–1503 and reprinted dozens of times

fuentes/mundus-novus/resumen.texto: Letter attributed to Vespucci that narrates the Portuguese voyage of 1501–1502 along the coast of Brazil and claims that these lands are a “new world,” distinct from Asia. It describes the Indigenous people as people without property or king, who ate their enemies.

fuentes/mundus-novus/por_que_importa.texto: It spread the idea of a new continent in Europe and was the basis for Waldseemüller giving that continent Vespucci's name. Several historians believe it was reworked or expanded by its editors.

fuentes/carta-a-soderini/titulo.texto: Letter from Amerigo Vespucci to Piero Soderini

fuentes/carta-a-soderini/soporte.texto: Printed in Florence around 1505; translated into Latin in the Cosmographiae Introductio (1507)

fuentes/carta-a-soderini/resumen.texto: Letter printed under Vespucci's name that recounts four voyages between 1497 and 1504. The first, of 1497, would have taken him to the mainland before Columbus. Most historians consider that first voyage nonexistent and the letter a compilation by other authors or editors.

fuentes/carta-a-soderini/por_que_importa.texto: It was the letter read by Waldseemüller and Ringmann, and it explains why they attributed the discovery of the continent to Vespucci.

fuentes/carta-a-soderini/leer.0.titulo.texto: 1916 reproduction of the 1505 «Lettera», with translation, Princeton University Press (Internet Archive)

fuentes/cosmographiae-introductio/soport.texto: Printed in Saint-Dié on April 25, 1507; probably written with Matthias Ringmann

fuentes/cosmographiae-introductio/resume.texto: Short treatise on cosmography that accompanied Waldseemüller's large world map and included the Latin translation of the letter to Soderini. In its ninth chapter it proposes calling the fourth part of the world “America,” the land of Amerigo, because Europe and Asia had women's names and he had discovered it.

fuentes/cosmographiae-introductio/por_qu.texto: It is the text in which the name America was born.

fuentes/cosmographiae-introductio/leer.0.texto: Facsimile with English translation (United States Catholic Historical Society, 1907), at Internet Archive

fuentes/mapa-de-waldseemuller/soporte.texto: Map printed on twelve sheets; the only known copy, found in 1901 at Wolfegg Castle, was bought by the Library of Congress of the United States in 2003

fuentes/mapa-de-waldseemuller/resumen.texto: World map on twelve sheets showing the New World as a strip of land separated from Asia by an ocean, with the name “America” written over the southern part. About a thousand copies were printed, of which only one is known.

fuentes/mapa-de-waldseemuller/por_que_im.texto: It is the first map with the name America and one of the first to represent an ocean west of the continent, before the Europeans reached the Pacific.

fuentes/mapa-de-juan-de-la-cosa/titulo.texto: Map of Juan de la Cosa

fuentes/mapa-de-juan-de-la-cosa/soporte.texto: Parchment held in the Naval Museum in Madrid

fuentes/mapa-de-juan-de-la-cosa/resumen.texto: Nautical chart of the world painted on parchment, showing alongside Europe, Africa and Asia the Antilles and the north coast of South America explored by 1500, with Cuba drawn as an island. It bears the signature of Juan de la Cosa and the date 1500, at El Puerto de Santa María.

fuentes/mapa-de-juan-de-la-cosa/por_que_.texto: It is the oldest surviving map with the lands found by Columbus and the first Andalusian voyages.

fuentes/mapa-de-juan-de-la-cosa/leer.0.t.texto: Images of the Juan de la Cosa map (Wikimedia Commons)

fuentes/provision-sobre-los-canibales-15.texto: Royal provision authorizing the capture of cannibals (October 30, 1503)

Provision of Isabella I which, after having prohibited the enslavement of Indians, authorizes making war on, capturing and selling as slaves the “cannibals” who resisted receiving Christians and ate human flesh, in islands of the Lesser Antilles and on the coast of Cartagena, in order to take them elsewhere and sell them.

It turned the accusation of cannibalism into a legal category. In the following decades shipowners declared peoples from across the region “Caribs” in order to enslave them, a practice the Dominicans denounced.

fuentes/cedula-de-medina-del-campo-1503/.texto: Real cédula on the labor of the Indians of Hispaniola (December 20, 1503)

Decree to Ovando which, upon a report that free Indians were fleeing contact with the Spaniards, orders that they be compelled to work in the mines, buildings and farms of the Christians for a wage, and to live in villages near them to be instructed, “as free persons, as they are, and not as serfs.”
It was the legal basis for the distribution of Indians among colonists that Ovando organized, and of the encomienda system in the Antilles: forced labor of people who were legally free.

fuentes/repartimiento-de-alburquerque-15.texto: Repartimiento of the Indians of Hispaniola of 1514
Rodrigo de Alburquerque and Pedro Ibáñez de Ibarra

Record of the general distribution of the Indians of Hispaniola among residents, officials and the Crown, made by the distributor Rodrigo de Alburquerque on the orders of Ferdinand the Catholic. It lists, town by town, the encomenderos and caciques with their Indians, which totaled some 26,000 people.

It is the best indirect census of the Taíno population twenty years after the arrival of the Spaniards, and it shows who kept Indigenous labor, including court officials who never set foot on the island.

fuentes/interrogatorio-jeronimo-1517/tit.texto: Hieronymite interrogation on the capacity of the Indians (1517)

fuentes/interrogatorio-jeronimo-1517/aut.texto: Luis de Figueroa, Alonso de Santo Domingo and Bernardino de Manzanedo

fuentes/interrogatorio-jeronimo-1517/res.texto: Survey that the three Hieronymite friars sent by Cisneros conducted with longtime residents of Hispaniola to find out whether the Indians could live on their own, free, in villages like the farmers of Castile. Nearly all the witnesses, beneficiaries of the encomiendas, answered that they could not.

fuentes/interrogatorio-jeronimo-1517/por.texto: It is a key document in the debate over the “capacity” of the Indians, and it shows how the interests of the encomenderos weighed on the answers.

fuentes/in-apostolatus-culmine/resumen.texto: Bull which, at the request of the Dominicans, raised their studium generale in Santo Domingo to a university with the privileges of Alcalá and Salamanca. The original is not preserved, and the text is known from later copies.

fuentes/in-apostolatus-culmine/por_que_i.texto: It is the document on which the claim of the University of Santo Domingo to be the first in America rests. Its validity without royal approval (pase real) was disputed against those of Lima and Mexico, founded by royal decree in 1551.

fuentes/in-apostolatus-culmine/leer.0.ti.texto: Opening of the Latin text of the bull, papalencyclicals.net

fuentes/true-and-exact-history-of-barbad.texto: A True and Exact History of the Island of Barbados

Account of the three years Ligon spent in Barbados, with a map of the island and plans of a sugar mill. It describes the shift from tobacco and cotton to sugar, the plantation economy, the work and punishments of contracted European servants and of African slaves, their meals and their music, and an attempted servant rebellion.
It is direct testimony of the “sugar revolution” that turned Barbados into the model of the English slave plantation colony.

fuentes/tratado-de-1660-con-los-caribes/.texto: Peace treaty among the French, the English and the Caribs (1660)
French and English governors of the Antilles and Kalinago chiefs
Signed at Basse-Terre (Guadeloupe) on March 31, 1660; we know its text through Du Tertre

Agreement signed after years of war between the French and English colonists and the Kalinago of the Lesser Antilles, who had been expelled from Martinique in 1658. The Kalinago agreed to leave the other islands, and in exchange Dominica and Saint Vincent were reserved for them.
It fixed for a century the division of the Lesser Antilles among European colonies and the two Indigenous islands, which the British occupied after 1763.

fuentes/codigo-de-esclavos-de-barbados/t.texto: Law for the better ordering and government of negroes (Barbados slave code)

fuentes/codigo-de-esclavos-de-barbados/r.texto: Law of the assembly of Barbados colonists which, in its preamble, calls Africans “heathenish, brutish and an uncertaine dangerous kinde of people” who had to be governed by laws of their own. It treats slaves as property, prohibits them from leaving the plantation without a pass, sets punishments of flogging, mutilation and death, and leaves almost unpunished the master who killed a slave while punishing him.

fuentes/codigo-de-esclavos-de-barbados/p.texto: It was the first comprehensive slave code of the English colonies and served as a model for those of Jamaica, Antigua and South Carolina.

fuentes/codigo-de-esclavos-de-barbados/l.texto: Transcription of the 1661 code (Slavery, Law, and Power)

fuentes/code-noir/autor.texto: Louis XIV (prepared under Colbert and his son Seignelay)

fuentes/code-noir/resumen.texto: Edict that regulated slavery in the French Antilles. It expels Jews from the islands, requires that slaves be baptized and instructed in the Catholic faith, prohibits making them work on Sundays and sets their food and clothing rations. It declares them movable property, allows them to be whipped, and punishes flight with the cutting of ears and branding, then with hamstringing and finally with death. It provides for punishing the master who killed a slave, allows masters to free slaves, and gives freedmen the same rights as those born free.

fuentes/code-noir/por_que_importa.texto: It is the central text of French slavery. Its defenders presented it as a minimal protection and its critics, such as Louis Sala-Molins, as the legalization of dehumanization. Prosecutions of masters for violating its protective articles were very rare.

fuentes/code-noir/leer.0.titulo.texto: Text of the 1685 edict at Wikisource

fuentes/histoire-generale-des-antilles/t.texto: General History of the Antilles Inhabited by the French

fuentes/histoire-generale-des-antilles/r.texto: Four-volume history of the French colonies of Saint Christopher, Guadeloupe and Martinique from 1625, with their conflicts with the English and the Kalinago, the massacre of 1626, the treaty of 1660, the life of the colonists, the contracted servants and African slaves, and the flora and fauna of the islands.

fuentes/histoire-generale-des-antilles/p.texto: It is the main source for the first half-century of the French Antilles and for the description of the Kalinago, written by a missionary who defended both evangelization and colonial order.

fuentes/dictionnaire-caraibe-francois/so.texto: Followed by a French-Carib dictionary (1666) and a grammar (1667)

fuentes/dictionnaire-caraibe-francois/re.texto: Dictionary of the language of the Kalinago of Dominica, with long notes on their life: the war with the Arawak and the Europeans, the treatment of prisoners, kinship, religion, and the difference between the speech of men and that of women, which the Kalinago themselves explained by the Arawak captive women taken in war.

fuentes/dictionnaire-caraibe-francois/po.texto: It is the richest source on the Kalinago language and society before their displacement by the Europeans.

fuentes/americaensche-zee-roovers/soport.texto: Translated into German (1679), Spanish (Cologne, 1681) and English (1684)

fuentes/americaensche-zee-roovers/resume.texto: Account by a surgeon who lived among the buccaneers of Tortuga and Jamaica. It describes the life of the cattle hunters of Hispaniola, the customs of the filibusters and the campaigns of L'Olonnais and Morgan in Maracaibo, Portobelo and Panama, with their sackings and the torture of prisoners.

fuentes/americaensche-zee-roovers/por_qu.texto: It is the basic source on the buccaneers. Morgan sued the English publishers for defamation, mainly for presenting him as a former contracted servant, and obtained compensation and a retraction.

fuentes/nouveau-voyage-aux-isles/titulo.texto: New Voyage to the Islands of America

fuentes/nouveau-voyage-aux-isles/resumen.texto: Six-volume account of Labat's stay in Martinique and Guadeloupe. It describes in detail the making of sugar and rum, the organization of the plantations, the African slaves, their punishments and their religion, the Kalinago of Dominica, the buccaneers and the war with the English.

fuentes/nouveau-voyage-aux-isles/por_que.texto: It is a first-rate technical and social source on the French slave plantation, written by an owner who considered it legitimate.

fuentes/tratado-con-los-cimarrones-de-so.texto: Peace treaty with the Leeward Maroons (1739)
Signed on March 1, 1739, by Cudjoe and Colonel John Guthrie; a similar treaty was signed in June with the Windward Maroons

Agreement that ended the first Maroon War in western Jamaica. It recognizes the freedom of Cudjoe and his people and grants them 1,500 acres of land. In return, the Maroons had to return runaway slaves, help the authorities against rebellions and invasions, and accept a white superintendent.

It was one of the first treaties in which a European power recognized the freedom of a community of runaway slaves, and at the same time turned the Maroons into allies of the slave system, as seen in 1760.

fuentes/history-of-jamaica-long/resumen.texto: History and description of Jamaica in three volumes: geography, government, economy, parishes, plants and inhabitants. It defends slavery and the slave trade, and devotes chapters to arguing that Africans were a distinct species, inferior and intellectually close to apes.

fuentes/history-of-jamaica-long/por_que_.texto: It is a rich source on eighteenth-century Jamaica and at the same time one of the most influential documents of the racist ideology of the British planters, cited for a century by defenders of slavery.

fuentes/interesting-narrative-equiano/ti.texto: The Interesting Narrative of the Life of Olaudah Equiano

fuentes/interesting-narrative-equiano/re.texto: Autobiography recounting the author's capture in Africa, the voyage on a slave ship, his enslavement in Virginia, in the British navy and in Montserrat, the purchase of his freedom, his travels and his conversion to Methodism. It describes the punishments, the sales and the sexual abuse on the islands, and proposes replacing the slave trade with trade with Africa.

fuentes/interesting-narrative-equiano/po.texto: It was a publishing success, with nine editions during the author's lifetime, and a weapon of British abolitionism. The debate over his birthplace affects the first chapters, not the rest of the account.

fuentes/description-de-saint-domingue/ti.texto: Description of the French Part of the Island of Santo Domingo

fuentes/description-de-saint-domingue/au.texto: Médéric Louis Élie Moreau de Saint-Méry

fuentes/description-de-saint-domingue/re.texto: Parish-by-parish description of the colony of Saint-Domingue on the eve of the revolution, with its population, plantations, towns, customs and castes. It includes a classification of people of mixed ancestry into categories according to the proportion of European and African ancestors.

fuentes/description-de-saint-domingue/po.texto: It is the main source on the richest colony in the Caribbean before 1791, and a document of how colonial society ranked people by color.

fuentes/description-de-saint-domingue/le.texto: Original edition (Philadelphia, 1797), volume 1, at Internet Archive

fuentes/ley-del-16-pluvioso-del-ano-ii/t.texto: Decree of the Convention of 16 Pluviôse, Year II (abolition of slavery in the colonies)

fuentes/ley-del-16-pluvioso-del-ano-ii/r.texto: Decree of the French National Convention that abolished slavery in all the colonies and declared all their inhabitants French citizens, without distinction of color. It ratified the abolition that the commissioners Sonthonax and Polverel had already proclaimed in Saint-Domingue in 1793.

fuentes/ley-del-16-pluvioso-del-ano-ii/p.texto: It was the first general abolition of slavery by a colonial power. It was applied only in Saint-Domingue, Guadeloupe and Guiana, and Napoleon annulled it in practice in 1802.

fuentes/ley-del-16-pluvioso-del-ano-ii/l.texto: Archives parlementaires, vol. LXXXIV: session of 16 Pluviôse, year II (Persée)

fuentes/constitucion-de-saint-domingue-1.texto: Constitution of the French colony of Saint-Domingue (1801)
Drafted by an assembly chosen by Toussaint and promulgated by him on July 8, 1801

Constitution that declares slavery abolished forever on the island, all its inhabitants equal without distinction of color, and Catholicism the religion of the colony. It names Toussaint governor for life, with the power to choose a successor, and obliges workers to remain on the plantations, whose production the colony needed.
It affirmed the autonomy of the colony without declaring independence, and Napoleon took it as a challenge. It also shows the compulsory labor that the new authority imposed on former slaves.

fuentes/ley-del-20-de-mayo-de-1802/titul.texto: Law of May 20, 1802, on slavery in the colonies

fuentes/ley-del-20-de-mayo-de-1802/resum.texto: Law of the Consulate that maintained slavery and the slave trade in the colonies returned to France by the Peace of Amiens, such as Martinique, where abolition had never been applied. That same year a consular decree restored slavery in Guadeloupe.

fuentes/ley-del-20-de-mayo-de-1802/por_q.texto: It showed the former slaves of Saint-Domingue that Leclerc's expedition sought to return them to slavery, and it turned the war into a struggle for independence.

fuentes/acta-de-independencia-de-haiti/s.texto: Proclaimed in Gonaïves on January 1, 1804; drafted by Louis Boisrond-Tonnerre. The only known printed copy was found by Julia Gaffield in 2010 in the National Archives of the United Kingdom

fuentes/acta-de-independencia-de-haiti/r.texto: Proclamation by Dessalines and his generals declaring the independence of the former colony under the Indigenous name of Haiti, and swearing to “renounce France forever” and to die before returning to its rule. It calls for vengeance against the French for their crimes.

fuentes/acta-de-independencia-de-haiti/p.texto: It founded the second independent state in the Americas and the first to arise from a slave rebellion.

fuentes/constitucion-de-haiti-1805/resum.texto: Constitution that makes Haiti an empire with Dessalines as emperor, forever prohibits slavery, and declares that no white person may own land in the country, except naturalized white women and the Germans and Poles who had joined the Haitian side. It establishes that all Haitians will be known as “blacks.”

fuentes/constitucion-de-haiti-1805/por_q.texto: It shows the break with the colonial order and the fear of a French reconquest, as well as the authoritarian power of the new emperor.

fuentes/constitucion-de-haiti-1805/leer..texto: Text of the imperial Constitution of 20 May 1805 (Haïti-Référence)

fuentes/aboriginal-population-of-hispani.texto: With Woodrow Borah, in Essays in Population History, volume 1 (Berkeley, University of California Press)

Study that, starting from the tribute figures of 1496, from the figure of 1,100,000 people that Las Casas attributes to a count by Bartholomew Columbus, and from the counts of 1508–1518, projects the curve of depopulation backward and arrives at a population of some 8 million inhabitants in 1492.

It is the highest estimate for Hispaniola and the most cited example of the Berkeley school. David Henige and Massimo Livi-Bacci criticized its assumptions, and most specialists consider it greatly exaggerated.

fuentes/contact-population-of-hispaniola.texto: On the Population of Hispaniola at the Time of Contact: History as Higher Mathematics

Article that examines the sources of the large population estimates for Hispaniola, especially those of Cook and Borah. It argues that the chroniclers' figures are unreliable and do not allow the population of 1492 to be calculated precisely.
It is the most influential methodological critique of the high figures of the Berkeley school for the Caribbean.

fuentes/return-to-hispaniola/titulo.texto: Return to Hispaniola: A Reassessment of a Demographic Catastrophe

fuentes/return-to-hispaniola/resumen.texto: Demographic study that estimates the Taíno population of Hispaniola in 1492 at a few hundred thousand (between 200,000 and 300,000), and explains its collapse until 1518 more by forced labor in the gold mines, the disorganization of food production, the separation of families and the drop in births than by epidemics, which according to the author arrived only with the smallpox of 1518.

fuentes/return-to-hispaniola/por_que_imp.texto: It is the standard demographic synthesis on Hispaniola, and it discusses both the figures in the millions and the explanation of depopulation by disease alone.

fuentes/despues-de-colon-moya-pons/titul.texto: After Columbus: Labor, Society and Politics in the Gold Economy

fuentes/despues-de-colon-moya-pons/resum.texto: Study of the gold economy of Hispaniola between 1493 and 1520: the tributes of the Columbus family, the repartimientos, Ovando's encomienda, the towns, the smelting works and the struggle for control of the Indians among the Columbus family, the Crown's officials and the colonists.

fuentes/despues-de-colon-moya-pons/por_q.texto: It explains the fall of the Taíno population within the mining economy that caused it, using the documents of the Royal Treasury.

fuentes/el-indio-antillano/titulo.texto: The Antillean Indian: Repartimiento, Encomienda and Slavery (1492–1542)

fuentes/el-indio-antillano/resumen.texto: Study, based on the General Archive of the Indies, of Indigenous labor in the Antilles: the repartimientos, the encomienda, the protective legislation, the enslavement of Indians declared Caribs or taken in a “just war,” the rescue expeditions to other islands and to Tierra Firme, and the trade in Indians to Hispaniola.

fuentes/el-indio-antillano/por_que_impor.texto: It shows with documents the distance between the protective laws and their application on the islands.

fuentes/the-tainos-rouse/titulo.texto: The Tainos: Rise and Decline of the People Who Greeted Columbus

fuentes/the-tainos-rouse/resumen.texto: Synthesis of Antillean archaeology from the first settlers: the Archaic migrations, the arrival of Saladoid farmers from the Orinoco around 500 BC, the Ostionoid development and the emergence of the classic Taínos, with their chiefdoms, their bateyes and their religion, up to their disappearance as a people under Spanish rule.

fuentes/the-tainos-rouse/por_que_importa.texto: For decades it was the reference model. Its critics, such as William Keegan and Corinne Hofman, dispute its scheme of peoples replacing one another through successive migrations.

fuentes/the-caribbean-before-columbus/au.texto: William F. Keegan and Corinne L. Hofman

fuentes/the-caribbean-before-columbus/re.texto: Updated synthesis of the archaeology of the pre-Columbian Caribbean, which replaces the model of migration waves with networks of exchange and movement among islands and the mainland, and describes the diversity of peoples that the word “Taíno” covers.

fuentes/the-caribbean-before-columbus/po.texto: It represents the recent archaeological consensus and revises the image of the Taínos inherited from the chroniclers.

fuentes/surviving-spanish-conquest/titul.texto: Surviving the Spanish Conquest: Resistance, Flight and Cultural Transformation of the Indians of Hispaniola and Puerto Rico

fuentes/surviving-spanish-conquest/resum.texto: Study, using documents and archaeology, of how the Taínos responded to the conquest: war, flight to the mountains, alliances, suicide, and marriage with Spaniards and Africans. It also shows the arrival in the Antilles of thousands of enslaved Indians from other islands and from Tierra Firme, who mixed with the survivors.

fuentes/surviving-spanish-conquest/por_q.texto: It challenges the idea of total extinction. Indigenous people disappeared from the records as a group, but they left descendants and culture in the Creole population.

fuentes/origins-and-genetic-legacies-of-.texto: Origins and Genetic Legacies of the Caribbean Taínos
Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 115 (10)

First complete ancient genome from the Antilles: that of a woman buried about a thousand years ago in Preacher's Cave, on Eleuthera (Bahamas). Her ancestry is closest to that of Arawak-speaking peoples of northern South America, which supports the continental origin of the Taínos, and part of that ancestry survives in present-day Puerto Ricans.
It confirmed with DNA the South American origin of the Taínos and the genetic continuity of Indigenous ancestry in the present-day population of the Antilles.

fuentes/genetic-history-of-the-pre-conta.texto: A Genetic History of the Precontact Caribbean
Daniel M. Fernandes and others (with David Reich)

Analysis of the DNA of 174 ancient individuals from the Bahamas, Hispaniola, Puerto Rico, Curaçao and Venezuela. It identifies at least two settlements: an Archaic one of hunter-gatherers, and another some 2,500 years ago of ceramic-making farmers related to peoples of northern South America, who mixed little with the earlier ones. From the amount of DNA shared among individuals it estimates that in the centuries before 1492 Hispaniola and Puerto Rico had populations on the order of tens of thousands of people.

It is the strongest scientific evidence against the figures of millions of inhabitants for Hispaniola. It is an indirect estimate, with wide margins, which the authors contrast with the chroniclers' figures, and it does not refer to the exact moment of contact.

fuentes/colonial-encounters-hulme/titulo.texto: Colonial Encounters: Europe and the Native Caribbean, 1492–1797

fuentes/colonial-encounters-hulme/resume.texto: Analysis of European texts on the Caribbean, from Columbus's diary to Shakespeare's The Tempest and to the deportation of the Garifuna. It argues that the opposition between peaceful Arawaks and cannibal Caribs was a construction of colonial discourse that served to justify war and slavery.

fuentes/colonial-encounters-hulme/por_qu.texto: It is a foundational work of postcolonial studies of the Caribbean. Its critics reproach it for underrating the ethnographic testimony on war and cannibalism.

fuentes/wild-majesty/titulo.texto: Wild Majesty: Encounters with the Caribs from Columbus to the Present

fuentes/wild-majesty/soporte.texto: With Peter Hulme; Oxford, Clarendon Press

fuentes/wild-majesty/resumen.texto: Annotated anthology of European and Carib texts on the Kalinago, from Columbus, Chanca and Cuneo to Breton, Du Tertre, the British reports on Saint Vincent and the Dominica reserve in the twentieth century.

fuentes/wild-majesty/por_que_importa.texto: It brings together in one volume the main sources on the Caribs of the islands, with discussion of their reliability.

fuentes/black-jacobins/resumen.texto: History of the Haitian revolution centered on Toussaint Louverture, which presents it as part of the French Revolution and as the first victorious revolution of slaves. It offers a Marxist reading of the colony's classes and an explicitly anticolonial thesis.

fuentes/black-jacobins/por_que_importa.texto: It was the work that placed the Haitian revolution at the center of Atlantic history. Its militant approach and its admiration for Toussaint are part of its method.

fuentes/avengers-of-the-new-world/titulo.texto: Avengers of the New World: The Story of the Haitian Revolution

fuentes/avengers-of-the-new-world/resume.texto: History of the Haitian revolution from the plantation society of Saint-Domingue to independence, covering slave rebellions, the conflicts of free people of color, the abolition of 1793–1794, Toussaint's government and the war against Leclerc.

fuentes/avengers-of-the-new-world/por_qu.texto: It is the standard academic synthesis on the revolution.

fuentes/haitian-revolutionary-studies/re.texto: Collection of studies on the Saint-Domingue revolution: the uprising of 1791, the Bois Caïman ceremony and its sources, the role of vodou, the British occupation, and Toussaint and independence, with extensive archival work.

fuentes/haitian-revolutionary-studies/po.texto: It establishes what the documents say about episodes turned into national myths, such as Bois Caïman.

fuentes/caribbean-genocide-girard/titulo.texto: Caribbean Genocide: Racial War in Haiti, 1802–1804

fuentes/caribbean-genocide-girard/resume.texto: Article that analyzes the final phase of Haiti's war of independence, in which both sides set out to eliminate the opposing group: the extermination campaign that Leclerc and Rochambeau proposed against the Black population, and the massacre of the French ordered by Dessalines in 1804. It discusses whether both cases fit the definition of genocide.

fuentes/caribbean-genocide-girard/por_qu.texto: It treats the violence of both sides with the same tools, which militant historiography usually recounts separately.

fuentes/equiano-the-african/titulo.texto: Equiano, the African: Biography of a Self-Made Man

fuentes/equiano-the-african/resumen.texto: Documentary biography of Olaudah Equiano presenting a baptism record and a naval list that give his birthplace as South Carolina, and suggesting that his account of his African childhood may have been built with testimony from others.

fuentes/equiano-the-african/por_que_impo.texto: It opened the debate over the authenticity of the first chapters of the Narrative, which other specialists, such as Paul Lovejoy, defend.

fuentes/la-caida-de-cristobal-colon/titu.texto: The Fall of Christopher Columbus: Bobadilla's Judgment

fuentes/la-caida-de-cristobal-colon/auto.texto: Consuelo Varela (with transcription by Isabel Aguirre)

fuentes/la-caida-de-cristobal-colon/resu.texto: Edition and study of Francisco de Bobadilla's inquiry against the Columbus family, found in Simancas, with the context of the government of Hispaniola between 1494 and 1500.

fuentes/la-caida-de-cristobal-colon/por_.texto: It made accessible a document that changed the image of the Columbian government, although its hostile origin requires that it be read with caution.

fuentes/vida-y-viajes-de-colon-irving/ti.texto: A History of the Life and Voyages of Christopher Columbus

fuentes/vida-y-viajes-de-colon-irving/so.texto: Published in London and New York in 1828, in four volumes

fuentes/vida-y-viajes-de-colon-irving/re.texto: Novelized biography of Columbus written by the American author Washington Irving, using documents that Martín Fernández de Navarrete had gathered in Madrid. It presents Columbus as a misunderstood modern hero and embellishes or invents scenes, among them a debate at Salamanca in which learned churchmen supposedly argued that the Earth was flat.

fuentes/vida-y-viajes-de-colon-irving/po.texto: It was widely read in the nineteenth century. It spread the myth that in 1492 people believed in a flat Earth, and it fixed the romantic image of Columbus in the United States.

fuentes/geschichte-der-mission-oldendorp.texto: History of the Mission of the Evangelical Brethren in the Caribbean Islands of Saint Thomas, Saint Croix and Saint John
Published in Barby in 1777 in an abridged version by Johann Jakob Bossart

Work by the Moravian missionary Oldendorp, who visited the Danish West Indies in 1767–1768. It recounts the Moravian mission among the slaves from 1732, describes the plantations, the treatment of slaves and their Dutch-based creole language, and records what slaves brought from various peoples of West Africa told him about their lands and languages.

It is a principal source on the slave society of the Danish islands in the eighteenth century and one of the first European descriptions of a creole language, written from a mission that did not question slavery.

fuentes/libro-de-las-profecias/resumen.texto: Compilation of biblical texts and of Christian authors on the end of times, gathered by Columbus after his third voyage, probably with the help of the Carthusian Gaspar Gorricio, between September 1501 and March 1502, with additions until around 1505. It contains the conditions that, according to medieval tradition, had to be met before the end of the world: the spread of Christianity, the discovery of the earthly Paradise, a final crusade that would recover Jerusalem, and a last world emperor, a role Columbus attributed to the Catholic Monarchs. It was influenced by medieval authors such as Joachim of Fiore.

fuentes/libro-de-las-profecias/por_que_i.texto: It shows that Columbus understood his enterprise within a prophetic scheme of the end of times, and not only as a search for trade routes and gold.

fuentes/libro-de-los-privilegios/resumen.texto: Book that Columbus finished in 1502, before his fourth voyage, prepared in Seville with the help of judges and notaries, to document the favors and privileges that he believed the crown owed to him and his heirs for having found a new route to the Indies and for the conquest and Christianization of the lands subjected. It contains a document in which Columbus calls the lands he found «the Western Indies» and says they were unknown to everyone, which some read as a sign that he knew he had found a new continent.

fuentes/libro-de-los-privilegios/por_que.texto: It is the documentary basis for the Columbus family's claims; after its preparation came the long Columbian lawsuits between the family and the crown.

fuentes/libro-de-los-privilegios/leer.0..texto: Facsimile with transcription and English translation (1893)

personas/guacanagari/resumen.texto: Cacique of Marién, in the northwest of Hispaniola. He helped Columbus when the Santa María was wrecked on Christmas Eve 1492, and allowed him to build the fort of La Navidad with the remains of the ship. When the Spaniards found the fort destroyed in November 1493, he blamed Caonabo. According to Hernando Colón and Las Casas he remained allied with the Spaniards in the war of 1495, which cost him the enmity of the other caciques.

personas/caonabo/resumen.texto: Cacique of Maguana, in the center of Hispaniola, to whom the Spaniards attributed the destruction of La Navidad and its garrison. Alonso de Ojeda captured him in 1495 through a ruse that Las Casas describes (metal shackles presented as an ornament), and he died around 1496 in the shipwreck of the vessel carrying him to Castile.

personas/guarionex/resumen.texto: Cacique of Maguá, in the Vega Real. Friar Ramón Pané lived near his village and baptized some of his servants. He rose against the gold tribute and was captured by Bartholomew Columbus around 1497–1498. He died in the shipwreck of the fleet of July 1502, while being taken prisoner to Castile.

personas/anacaona/resumen.texto: Sister of Behechio, cacique of Jaragua in the west of Hispaniola, and wife of Caonabo. The chronicles remember her as a composer of areítos (ritual songs and dances) and as an ally of the first colonists; she succeeded her brother. Ovando seized her in the massacre of Jaragua and had her hanged in Santo Domingo, around 1503 or 1504.

personas/cotubanama/resumen.texto: Cacique of Higüey, at the eastern end of Hispaniola. He confronted the Spaniards in the wars of 1502 and 1503–1504. Juan de Esquivel captured him on the island of Saona and he was hanged in Santo Domingo, ending the organized resistance in the east of the island.

personas/agueybana-ii/resumen.texto: Cacique of the south of Borinquén (Puerto Rico), relative and successor of the Agüeybaná who received Ponce de León in 1508. He led the uprising of 1511, in which the encomendero Cristóbal de Sotomayor and other colonists died. According to tradition he died in combat that year, although the sources are not precise.

personas/hatuey/resumen.texto: Cacique of Guahabá, in Hispaniola, who went to Cuba with his people and led the resistance against Diego Velázquez's expedition in the east of the island. Captured, he was burned alive near Yara in early 1512. Las Casas, who did not witness it, recounts in the Brevísima that at the stake he refused baptism when he learned that there were Spaniards in heaven. The scene became a national symbol in Cuba.

personas/enriquillo/resumen.texto: Taíno cacique of the Bahoruco region, educated by the Franciscans of Verapaz. According to Las Casas, around 1519 he rose in the mountains after the abuses of his encomendero. He resisted for about fourteen years and in 1533 agreed with Francisco de Barrionuevo, an envoy of Charles V, to a pardon and freedom for himself and his people, who settled in Boyá. He died around 1535. His story was the subject of the novel Enriquillo by Manuel de Jesús Galván (1882).

personas/cristobal-colon/roles.2.texto: viceroy and governor of the Indies

personas/cristobal-colon/resumen.texto: Navigator, almost certainly from Genoa, who with the support of the Catholic Monarchs reached the Bahamas on October 12, 1492, and in four voyages (1492–1504) explored the Antilles and the coasts of Venezuela and Central America. As viceroy and governor of Hispaniola he imposed a gold tribute on the Taínos, sent captives to be sold in Castile, and had to make agreements with rebel colonists. In 1500 Francisco de Bobadilla removed him from office and sent him prisoner to Spain. He died in Valladolid, maintaining that his lands were part of Asia.

personas/bartolome-colon/resumen.texto: Brother of Christopher Columbus and adelantado of the Indies from 1497. He governed Hispaniola in his brother's absence (1496–1498), founded Santo Domingo on the east bank of the Ozama, demanded tribute from the chiefdoms, captured Guarionex and confronted the rebellion of Francisco Roldán. In 1500 he was sent prisoner to Castile with his brother.

personas/diego-colon/resumen.texto: Eldest son of Christopher Columbus and second admiral of the Indies. After the Columbian lawsuits he was governor of Hispaniola from 1509. He organized the occupation of Cuba, Puerto Rico and Jamaica and built the Alcázar of Santo Domingo. On his sugar mill the rebellion of enslaved Africans of 1521 broke out. The Crown gradually cut back his powers, and in 1523 it recalled him to Spain.

personas/hernando-colon/resumen.texto: Natural son of Christopher Columbus and Beatriz Enríquez de Arana. He accompanied his father on the fourth voyage (1502–1504), gathered in Seville a library of some 15,000 books, the basis of the Colombina Library, and wrote a life of his father that is known through the Italian translation published in Venice in 1571.

personas/francisco-de-bobadilla/resumen.texto: Commander of the Order of Calatrava sent by the Catholic Monarchs in 1500 as inquiry judge and governor of the Indies. He removed Christopher Columbus and his brothers from office, sent them prisoner to Castile together with the inquiry into their government, and facilitated colonists' access to gold and to Indians. He died in the shipwreck of the fleet in the hurricane of July 1502.

personas/francisco-roldan/resumen.texto: Chief magistrate of Hispaniola appointed by Columbus, who in 1497 rebelled against the Columbus brothers with part of the colonists and settled in Jaragua. In 1498–1499 Columbus had to make an agreement with him, restore him to his post and assign caciques and Indians to serve his men. This was a direct precedent for the repartimientos. He died in the shipwreck of 1502.

personas/martin-alonso-pinzon/resumen.texto: Shipowner from Palos who recruited much of the crew of the first voyage and captained the Pinta. In November 1492 he separated from Columbus to search for gold on his own and rejoined him in January 1493. He died in Palos soon after the return.

personas/ramon-pane/resumen.texto: Catalan friar of the Order of Saint Jerome who arrived in Hispaniola on Columbus's second voyage. At Columbus's request he lived among the Macorix and then in the chiefdom of Guarionex, learned the language, and around 1498 wrote an account of the beliefs of the Taínos, the first description of an American religion by a European based on living among its people. His dates of birth and death are unknown.

personas/diego-alvarez-chanca/resumen.texto: Physician from Seville to the Catholic Monarchs who traveled on Columbus's second voyage. His letter to the cabildo of Seville (1494) describes the arrival in the Lesser Antilles, the Carib villages of Guadeloupe and the founding of La Isabela, and it is the first European medical and naturalist text written in America.

personas/michele-da-cuneo/resumen.texto: Nobleman from Savona, friend of Columbus, who traveled on the second voyage. In a letter of 1495 he recounted, among other things, that he raped a Carib woman whom Columbus had given him as a slave, and the shipment of Taíno captives to Castile in February 1495. His text, preserved in Bologna, became known only in the nineteenth century.

personas/juan-de-la-cosa/resumen.texto: Sailor from Cantabria, author of the map of 1500, the oldest surviving map with the lands found by Columbus. He sailed on Columbus's second voyage and with Ojeda in 1499. It is debated whether he is the same Juan de la Cosa who owned the Santa María in 1492. He died in 1510 in a fight with Indigenous people near Turbaco, on Ojeda's expedition to Tierra Firme.

personas/americo-vespucio/resumen.texto: Florentine who worked in Seville for the Medici and supplied fleets to the Indies. He took part in at least two voyages, with Ojeda along the coast of Venezuela (1499) and in the service of Portugal along the coast of Brazil (1501–1502). The printed letters under his name attribute other voyages to him, which are disputed. He was chief pilot of the Casa de Contratación from 1508, and his name gave rise to the name America.

personas/pedro-martir-de-angleria/roles..texto: adviser to the Council of the Indies

personas/pedro-martir-de-angleria/resume.texto: Lombard humanist in the service of the Catholic Monarchs and of Charles V who, without ever traveling to America, wrote the Decades of the New World in Latin, based on conversations with Columbus and other navigators and on the papers arriving at the court. He was a member of the Council of the Indies from 1518 or 1520.

personas/gonzalo-fernandez-de-oviedo/res.texto: Official and chronicler from Madrid who spent much of his life in America: inspector of the gold smelters of Castilla del Oro from 1514, alcaide of the fortress of Santo Domingo from 1533, and official chronicler of the Indies from 1532. He wrote the Sumario de la natural historia (1526) and the General and Natural History of the Indies. His very negative judgment of the Indians, his defense of the conquistadors and his position as a beneficiary of the colonial system set him against Las Casas.

personas/nicolas-de-ovando/resumen.texto: Governor of the Indies from 1502 to 1509. He arrived with a fleet of some thirty ships and about 2,500 colonists. He refounded Santo Domingo on the west bank of the Ozama, founded towns and the hospital of San Nicolás, and organized the forced labor of Indians under the decree of 1503. He also led the massacre of Jaragua (1503) and the war of Higüey, and during his government the transfer of Lucayans as labor began.

personas/francisco-jimenez-de-cisneros/r.texto: Franciscan, archbishop of Toledo, grand inquisitor and regent of Castile in 1506–1507 and 1516–1517. As regent he listened to Las Casas, appointed him protector of the Indians, and sent three Hieronymite friars to govern Hispaniola with instructions to gather the Indians into free villages. He founded the University of Alcalá.

personas/juan-rodriguez-de-fonseca/resum.texto: Court cleric who from 1493 organized the fleets and affairs of the Indies, first on commission from the Catholic Monarchs and then from the Casa de Contratación (1503) and the Council of the Indies. He was an adversary of Columbus and of Las Casas, who accused him of protecting the interests of the encomenderos.

personas/pedro-de-cordoba/resumen.texto: Vicar of the first Dominicans who arrived in Hispaniola in 1510. He supported Antonio de Montesinos's sermon (1511), defended the freedom of the Indians before Ferdinand the Catholic, and wrote a Christian doctrine for their instruction that was printed in Mexico in 1544.

personas/juan-ponce-de-leon/resumen.texto: Arrived in Hispaniola in 1493 and took part in the war of Higüey. From 1508 he occupied Borinquén, founded Caparra and was governor of Puerto Rico, where he suppressed the Taíno uprising of 1511. In 1513 he reached Florida, and he died in Havana in 1521 from a wound received on his second voyage to that peninsula. The “fountain of youth” does not appear in his capitulation of 1512 or in the documents of his voyages. Later chroniclers associated it with him: Oviedo, who tells it mockingly, and Herrera (1601).

personas/diego-velazquez-de-cuellar/resu.texto: Took part in Ovando's wars in Hispaniola and from 1511 led the occupation of Cuba, where he founded Baracoa, Bayamo, Trinidad, Sancti Spíritus, Havana and Santiago. As governor he organized the expeditions to Mexico of Córdoba, Grijalva and Cortés, and later sent Pánfilo de Narváez against Cortés.

personas/juan-de-esquivel/resumen.texto: Led the last campaign against Higüey (1504), in which he captured Cotubanamá. In 1509 Diego Columbus sent him to occupy Jamaica, where he founded Sevilla la Nueva and became its first governor.

personas/martin-waldseemuller/resumen.texto: German cartographer of the humanist circle of Saint-Dié, in Lorraine. With Matthias Ringmann he published in 1507 the Cosmographiae Introductio and a large world map in which, for the first time, the southern lands were called America in honor of Amerigo Vespucci. In his Carta marina of 1516 he no longer used that name.

personas/thomas-warner/resumen.texto: English captain who founded in 1624 on Saint Christopher (Saint Kitts) the first stable English colony in the Antilles, which he shared with d'Esnambuc's French. Together with them he attacked the island's Kalinago in 1626, and he promoted the colonization of Nevis, Antigua and Montserrat. His son with a Kalinago woman, Thomas “Indian” Warner, was a Carib chief in Dominica and was killed in 1676 by an expedition led by his English half-brother.

personas/pierre-belain-d-esnambuc/resume.texto: Norman privateer who established a French colony in 1625 on Saint Christopher, next to Warner's English one, and took part with him in the attack on the Kalinago in 1626. With the support of Richelieu he founded the Company of Saint Christopher (1626) and, in 1635, the colony of Martinique, at Saint-Pierre.

personas/jean-baptiste-du-tertre/resumen.texto: French Dominican who lived, with interruptions, in Guadeloupe and Martinique between 1640 and 1658. His Histoire générale des Antilles (1667–1671) is the main source on the first decades of the French colonies, their wars with the Kalinago, slavery, and the nature of the islands.

personas/raymond-breton/resumen.texto: French Dominican who lived about twelve years in all among the Kalinago of Dominica, without achieving lasting conversions. He wrote a Carib-French dictionary (1665), a French-Carib dictionary (1666), a grammar and a catechism, the main sources on the language and society of the seventeenth-century Kalinago.

personas/jean-baptiste-labat/resumen.texto: French Dominican who managed his order's sugar plantation in Martinique, with its slaves, improved its mill and directed fortifications in Guadeloupe. His Nouveau voyage aux isles de l'Amérique (1722) describes island life, the Kalinago, the buccaneers and slavery, including punishments, from the point of view of an owner.

personas/richard-ligon/resumen.texto: English royalist who, after the civil war, spent three years in Barbados (1647–1650), at the moment when the island was shifting from tobacco to sugar. His A True and Exact History of the Island of Barbados (1657) describes the sugar mills, the work of contracted European servants and African slaves, and their rebellions.

personas/henry-morgan/resumen.texto: Welsh privateer with a commission from the government of Jamaica who sacked Puerto Príncipe (Cuba) and Portobelo in 1668, Maracaibo in 1669 and Panama in 1671. Exquemelin described the torture of prisoners in those campaigns. He was sent prisoner to London for violating the peace of 1670 with Spain, but returned knighted and as lieutenant governor of Jamaica (1674), where he pursued pirates.

personas/alexandre-exquemelin/resumen.texto: Frenchman who arrived in Tortuga around 1666 as a contracted servant of the French West India Company and later became surgeon to the buccaneers, with whom he took part in Morgan's campaigns. His book De Americaensche Zee-Roovers (Amsterdam, 1678) permanently fixed the image of the buccaneers.

personas/edward-long/resumen.texto: Jamaican planter and judge who owned slaves, and who wrote The History of Jamaica (1774). His work combines a detailed description of the island with a defense of slavery and a theory presenting Africans as a distinct and inferior species, widely cited later by pseudoscientific racism.

personas/olaudah-equiano/resumen.texto: Author of an autobiography (1789) in which he says he was born in Igbo land and was captured as a child. He was a slave of a British navy officer and of Robert King, a Quaker merchant from Philadelphia with business in Montserrat, from whom he bought his freedom in 1766. He then took part in the abolitionist movement in London. Vincent Carretta found a baptism record and a naval record that give his birthplace as South Carolina, and his birthplace is disputed.

personas/cudjoe/resumen.texto: Chief of the Leeward Maroons, in western Jamaica, during the first Maroon War. In 1739 he signed a treaty with the British recognizing the freedom and lands of his people, in exchange for returning runaway slaves and helping to suppress rebellions.

personas/nanny-de-los-cimarrones/resumen.texto: Leader of the Windward Maroons, in eastern Jamaica, in the first half of the eighteenth century. British documents mention her little (a 1740 land grant to “Nanny” and her followers). Her figure grew through oral tradition, and in the 1970s Jamaica declared her a national heroine.

personas/joseph-chatoyer/resumen.texto: Chief of the Black Caribs (Garifuna) of Saint Vincent. He fought the British in the first Carib war (1772–1773), which ended with a treaty under which they ceded part of their lands, and in 1795, with French support, he led the uprising in which he was killed in combat on March 14 of that year.

personas/moreau-de-saint-mery/nombre.texto: Médéric Louis Élie Moreau de Saint-Méry

personas/moreau-de-saint-mery/resumen.texto: Creole lawyer from Martinique who practiced in Cap-Français, compiled the laws of the French colonies and defended the colonists' interests in the Paris Assembly. His Description de la partie française de Saint-Domingue (1797) is the main description of the colony before the revolution and includes a classification of people according to their proportion of European ancestry.

personas/francois-mackandal/resumen.texto: Enslaved man of African origin, a Maroon in northern Saint-Domingue, accused of leading a network of poisonings against colonists and enslaved people. He was burned alive in Cap-Français in January 1758. Historians debate how much was a real conspiracy and how much was the colonists' panic over deaths from other causes. His figure became part of Haitian tradition.

personas/vincent-oge/roles.1.texto: leader of the free people of color

personas/vincent-oge/resumen.texto: Free merchant of color from Saint-Domingue who, in Paris, demanded equal political rights for free people of color. In October 1790 he rose in the north with a few hundred men, without calling for the abolition of slavery. Defeated and handed over by the Spaniards, he was broken on the wheel in Cap-Français in February 1791.

personas/dutty-boukman/resumen.texto: Enslaved man, according to tradition brought from Jamaica, who was one of the leaders of the uprising of August 1791 on the Northern Plain of Saint-Domingue, and whom later accounts associate with the Bois Caïman ceremony. He died in combat in November 1791, and his head was displayed in Cap-Français.

personas/leger-felicite-sonthonax/resume.texto: Jacobin lawyer sent to Saint-Domingue as civil commissioner in 1792. Harassed by the colonists, the British and the Spaniards, he proclaimed on August 29, 1793, the freedom of the slaves of the North to win them to the cause of the Republic. The Convention extended abolition to all the colonies in February 1794.

personas/toussaint-louverture/resumen.texto: Born enslaved on the Bréda plantation, near Cap-Français, he was free by about 1776 and, according to documents found in the 1970s, came to lease an estate with slaves. He joined the rebellion of 1791, fought for Spain and in 1794 switched to abolitionist France. He expelled the British (1798), defeated Rigaud in the War of the South (1799–1800), occupied Santo Domingo (1801) and issued a constitution that made him governor for life and tied workers to the plantations. Captured by deception by Leclerc in 1802, he died as a prisoner in the Fort de Joux.

personas/jean-jacques-dessalines/resumen.texto: Born enslaved, he was Toussaint's lieutenant and, after Toussaint's deportation, the leader of the war against the French expedition, which ended with the victory at Vertières (1803). He proclaimed Haiti's independence on January 1, 1804, ordered the massacre of the remaining French, and crowned himself emperor as Jacques I. He kept forced labor on the plantations and was assassinated by his own officers in October 1806.

personas/charles-leclerc/resumen.texto: French general, Napoleon's brother-in-law, who led the expedition sent in 1802 to restore French authority in Saint-Domingue. He captured Toussaint through deception and deported him; in his letters to Napoleon that year he proposed exterminating the Black people of the mountains, men and women, except the children. He died of yellow fever in November 1802.

personas/donatien-de-rochambeau/resumen.texto: Leclerc's successor in command of the French expedition. His campaign included mass executions, drownings and the use of attack dogs brought from Cuba, according to French testimonies of the time; defeated at Vertières, he capitulated and surrendered to the British fleet in November 1803.

personas/alexandre-petion/resumen.texto: Free man of color, an officer with Rigaud and later in the war of independence. After Dessalines's death he presided over the republic of the south and west of Haiti (1807–1818), distributed state lands in parcels and in 1816 helped Bolívar with weapons and ships in exchange for Bolívar freeing the enslaved people on the lands he took.

personas/henri-christophe/resumen.texto: Revolutionary general who, after Dessalines's death, governed northern Haiti, from 1811 as King Henry I. Using forced labor, he built the Citadelle Laferrière and the Sans-Souci palace and issued the Código Henri (1812); he killed himself in 1820 amid a rebellion.

personas/irving-rouse/resumen.texto: Yale archaeologist who established the ceramic chronology of the Antilles (Saladoid, Ostionoid, Chicoid) and the model of migrations from the Orinoco; he summarized his work in The Tainos (1992).

personas/frank-moya-pons/resumen.texto: Dominican historian, author of studies on the gold economy, the encomienda and the decline of the population of Hispaniola in the 16th century, and of textbooks on Dominican and Caribbean history.

personas/c-l-r-james/resumen.texto: Trinidadian writer who, in The Black Jacobins (1938), told the Haitian revolution from a Marxist and anticolonial perspective, with Toussaint as its protagonist; he was also a Trotskyist theorist and a cricket chronicler.

personas/laurent-dubois/resumen.texto: American historian of the Haitian revolution and of the French Caribbean, author of Avengers of the New World (2004).

personas/philippe-girard/resumen.texto: French historian specializing in the Haitian revolution, author of studies on Leclerc's expedition, the 1804 massacre and a biography of Toussaint Louverture (2016).

personas/jean-pierre-boyer/resumen.texto: Born in Port-au-Prince, son of a French tailor and of an African woman who had formerly been enslaved. In the War of the South (1799–1800) he sided with André Rigaud against Toussaint Louverture and left with him for France; he returned with Leclerc's expedition (1802) and went over to the insurgent leaders, Pétion and Dessalines, when it became known that France would restore slavery. He succeeded Pétion in 1818, reunited the country in 1820 and in February 1822 occupied the Spanish part of the island, independent since December 1821, so that he governed all of Hispaniola until his fall in 1843: Haitian historiography calls it unification, and Dominican historiography calls it occupation or Haitian domination. In 1825 he accepted Charles X's ordinance, presented by a French squadron off Port-au-Prince, which recognized independence in exchange for 150 million francs (90 million from 1838).

personas/bernardo-de-balbuena/resumen.texto: Spanish poet raised in New Spain («Grandeza mexicana», 1604; «El Bernardo», 1624). Appointed abbot of Jamaica in 1608, he reached the island in 1611 and failed to get it made a bishopric; bishop of Puerto Rico from 1620, he arrived in 1623, and in the Dutch attack of 1625 he lost his house and his library, which was burned. He died in San Juan in 1627. His year of birth varies by source (around 1561, 1562 or 1568).

personas/sanite-belair/resumen.texto: Freedwoman born in Verrettes, married in 1796 to Charles Bélair, nephew and aide of Toussaint Louverture; she rose to sergeant and then lieutenant in the fight against the French expedition. Captured by a column under Faustin Répussard together with her husband, she was sentenced to death on 5 October 1802: he was shot, and because of her sex she was given beheading instead. According to tradition she died before the firing squad, crying «Long live liberty, down with slavery!» and refusing to be blindfolded.

hechos/poblamiento-arcaico-de-las-antill.texto: The First Settlers of the Antilles

Hunters, fishers and gatherers reached Trinidad about 7,000 years ago and Cuba and Hispaniola around 4000 BC, with chipped and polished stone tools and, at some sites, early crops and pottery. Their origin is debated: because of their stone technology they were linked to Central America, and because of other traits to northern South America. Ancient DNA (Fernandes and others, 2021) shows that they formed a population distinct from the farmers who arrived later and that they mixed little with them.

hechos/cultura-saladoide/titulo.texto: The Saladoids, the First Ceramic-Making Farmers of the Islands

hechos/cultura-saladoide/resumen.texto: Cassava farmers and potters with white-on-red painted ceramics who arrived from the lower Orinoco to Trinidad, the Lesser Antilles and Puerto Rico around 500 BC. They lived in circular villages around a plaza where they buried their dead, and traded semiprecious stones over long distances. It is debated whether the groups called Huecoid, from Vieques, were an earlier or a parallel migration.

hechos/pueblo-taino/resumen.texto: Name given by scholars from the 19th century onward to the Arawak-speaking peoples of the Greater Antilles and the Bahamas; the word appears in the chronicles as “nitaíno,” the noble stratum. They grew cassava, from which they made casabe, as well as maize, sweet potato and cotton in mounds of earth (conucos); they lived in villages governed by caciques, with nitaínos and naborías, played the ballgame in bateyes and venerated cemíes with the cohoba rite. They waged war between chiefdoms and against the Caribs, and Oviedo claims that some women were buried alive with their cacique, a detail archaeology has not confirmed; their descendants survive in the present-day population of the Antilles.

hechos/cacicazgos-de-la-espanola/resumen.texto: According to Las Casas, in 1492 Hispaniola was divided into five large chiefdoms: Marién (Guacanagarí), Maguá (Guarionex), Maguana (Caonabo), Jaragua (Behechio and Anacaona) and Higüey (Cayacoa and, after his death, Cotubanamá), with lesser caciques subject to them. Other chroniclers mention more lordships, and archaeology does not allow borders to be fixed, so the scheme of five “kingdoms” is considered a simplification written decades later. In the north also lived the Ciguayos and the Macorix, who spoke other languages.

hechos/pueblo-lucayo/resumen.texto: People related to the Taíno who settled the Bahamas and the Turks and Caicos Islands from around 700–800 AD, having arrived from Hispaniola or Cuba. They were the first Americans Columbus encountered, at Guanahaní, and his diary is the only direct description of them. Between 1509 and 1520 the Spaniards took them to Hispaniola as labor and to the pearl fisheries of Cubagua, and the islands were left depopulated; the figure of some 40,000 people transported given by Peter Martyr cannot be verified.

hechos/pueblo-guanahatabey/resumen.texto: People of western Cuba whom Spanish sources, such as a letter from Diego Velázquez of 1514 and Las Casas, describe as living in caves, without agriculture and speaking a language different from Taíno. Rouse and others considered them survivors of the Archaic; Keegan and other archaeologists point out that no sites of theirs from that period have been identified and that the description is secondhand, so their existence as a separate people is debated.

hechos/pueblo-kalinago/resumen.texto: People of the Lesser Antilles, from Grenada to Guadeloupe, whom the Spaniards called “caribes,” a word from which “cannibal” derives. They spoke an Arawak language with a masculine vocabulary of Carib origin, which Breton attributed to women being descended from captive Arawak; they lived in villages of communal houses and made war expeditions by canoe against the Taíno and later against Europeans, taking captives. They resisted occupation until the 18th century; their descendants live in the Kalinago Territory of Dominica, created as a reserve in 1903.

hechos/canibalismo-caribe/titulo.texto: The Accusation of Cannibalism Against the Caribs

hechos/canibalismo-caribe/resumen.texto: In 1492 Columbus noted what the Taíno told him about the “caniba,” and in 1493 Chanca and Cuneo described human bones in houses on Guadeloupe, Taíno women held captive and castrated boys; Chanca says that in one house they found a man's neck cooking in a pot, although no one saw human flesh being eaten. The 1503 provision allowed enslaving cannibals, and from then on slave raiders also called “caribs” peoples who resisted without any evidence that they ate human flesh, which the Dominicans denounced. William Arens (1979) argued that there was no reliable evidence of cannibalism, and Peter Hulme and Jalil Sued Badillo saw the figure of the cannibal Carib as a colonial construction; Neil Whitehead and others accept the ritual consumption of parts of enemies, which Breton and Du Tertre describe in the 17th century as a past or rare custom.

hechos/adn-antiguo-de-las-antillas/titul.texto: What Ancient DNA Says About the Population of the Antilles

hechos/adn-antiguo-de-las-antillas/resum.texto: Studies by Schroeder and others (2018) and Fernandes and others (2021) confirmed that the Taíno descended from farmers who arrived from northern South America and that their ancestry is still present in Puerto Ricans, Dominicans and Cubans. Based on shared DNA, Fernandes and his team estimated that Hispaniola and Puerto Rico had populations in the tens of thousands in the centuries before 1492. That figure contrasts with those of Las Casas (more than three million), Cook and Borah (around eight million), Livi-Bacci (200,000 to 300,000) and Rosenblat (around 100,000 for Hispaniola); geneticists warn that it is an indirect estimate with wide margins.

hechos/fuerte-de-la-navidad/resumen.texto: After the wreck of the Santa María on Christmas Eve 1492, Columbus built a fort from its remains on the lands of Guacanagarí and left 39 men there. In November 1493 he found it burned and the men dead; Guacanagarí blamed Caonabo, and accounts gathered by Chanca and Hernando Columbus say that the Spaniards had quarreled among themselves and had taken women and gold from the Taíno.

hechos/segundo-viaje-de-colon/resumen.texto: Fleet of 17 ships with some 1,200 or 1,500 men, animals, seeds and sugarcane that left Cádiz in September 1493 to settle Hispaniola. It sailed through the Lesser Antilles and Puerto Rico, found La Navidad destroyed, founded La Isabela and explored the south coast of Cuba, which Columbus made his men swear was mainland, and Jamaica. During the voyage they began the war against the Taíno, the gold tribute and the shipment of captives to Castile; Columbus returned in 1496.

hechos/fundacion-de-la-isabela/resumen.texto: Columbus founded La Isabela in January 1494 on the north coast of Hispaniola, the first Spanish town in the Americas, hoping to exploit the gold of the Cibao. Disease, the lack of European food, the forced labor of the settlers and their rebellions made it fail, and around 1496–1498 the population moved to Santo Domingo. Excavations by Cruxent and Deagan revealed a town planned in the Castilian manner, with houses of stone and rammed earth and local pottery production.

hechos/batalla-de-la-vega-real/resumen.texto: Clash of March 1495 in which some two hundred Spaniards with horses and dogs, supported by Guacanagarí, defeated a coalition of caciques from the center of Hispaniola. Chronicles speak of tens of thousands of Indians, figures historians consider exaggerated.
