A later tradition attributes the victory to an apparition of the Virgin of Mercy on the Santo Cerro; after the defeat the gold tribute was imposed.

hechos/tributo-en-oro-de-los-colon/resum.texto: After the 1495 war Columbus required every Taíno over fourteen in the gold-bearing areas to deliver a small bell full of gold dust every three months, and in the other areas an arroba of cotton; whoever paid received a metal token to hang around the neck. The tribute was impossible to meet and many fled to the mountains; Las Casas claims that the Taíno stopped planting so that the Spaniards would go hungry, and that the famine of 1495–1496 killed mainly the Indians themselves.

hechos/venta-de-cautivos-tainos-en-casti.texto: Sale of Taíno Captives in Castile

In February 1495 Columbus shipped some 550 captives from La Isabela to sell them in Seville; according to Cuneo about 200 died on the voyage. Already in January 1494, in the memorial he sent with Antonio de Torres, Columbus had proposed paying for the colony's livestock and supplies with enslaved Caribs; the monarchs suspended the sales until theologians were consulted, and in June 1500 ordered that the Indians sold in Andalusia be returned to their land, although the enslavement of those taken in a “just war” remained permitted.

hechos/rebelion-de-roldan/resumen.texto: The chief magistrate Francisco Roldán rose up in 1497 against Bartolomé Columbus with part of the settlers, who demanded freedom to search for gold and to have Indians in their service, and settled in Jaragua. To end the conflict, Columbus made a pact with him in 1498–1499: he reinstated him in his post and assigned his men caciques and their towns to work for them, the precedent for the repartimientos and the Antillean encomienda.

hechos/tercer-viaje-de-colon/resumen.texto: Columbus left Sanlúcar in May 1498, reached Trinidad on July 31 and sailed through the Gulf of Paria, the first European contact with the mainland of South America; because of the volume of fresh water from the Orinoco he wrote that there was an immense land there and perhaps the earthly Paradise. On arriving at Santo Domingo he found Roldán's rebellion, and the voyage ended with his removal from office.

hechos/destitucion-de-colon/resumen.texto: Francisco de Bobadilla arrived in Santo Domingo in August 1500 with powers as a judge of inquiry, found Spaniards hanged on the orders of the Columbus family, took over the government and sent Cristóbal, Bartolomé and Diego Columbus in chains to Castile. The monarchs freed them in December, but did not return the government to Columbus, which passed to Nicolás de Ovando. The inquiry, found in the Archivo de Simancas and published in 2006, records the charges the settlers brought against the Columbus family, from witnesses hostile to them.

hechos/cuarto-viaje-de-colon/resumen.texto: Columbus, who was forbidden to land at Santo Domingo, warned Ovando of the hurricane of 1502 and then sailed the coast of Central America from Honduras to Panama looking for a passage to Asia. With his ships destroyed, he was stranded in Jamaica from June 1503 to June 1504; Diego Méndez crossed in a canoe to Hispaniola to ask for help, which Ovando delayed. Hernando Columbus recounts that his father used the lunar eclipse of February 29, 1504 to intimidate the Taíno, who had stopped giving them food.

hechos/huracan-de-1502/resumen.texto: In July 1502 a hurricane sank most of the fleet leaving Santo Domingo for Castile, with some 20 ships and hundreds of men, among them Francisco de Bobadilla, Francisco Roldán and the cacique Guarionex, and a large cargo of gold. It also destroyed the town, which Ovando rebuilt on the western bank of the Ozama.

hechos/gobierno-de-ovando/resumen.texto: Ovando arrived in April 1502 with some 2,500 settlers and over seven years founded about fifteen towns, the San Nicolás hospital and the new Santo Domingo, organized the exploitation of the gold mines and distributed Indians in encomienda. He subdued the remaining chiefdoms with the massacres of Jaragua and Higüey and began the transfer of the Lucayans. Historiography presents him both as the organizer of the first colonial order and as the governor under whom the Taíno population collapsed.

hechos/encomienda-en-la-espanola/resumen.texto: System by which the Crown assigned groups of Indians, legally free, to a settler who could use their labor in the mines, estates and households in exchange for feeding and clothing them and having them instructed in the faith. The Laws of Burgos (1512) set shifts of five months in the mines, rest periods and rations, but inspection records and lawsuits show exhausting workdays, separation of families and high mortality. The New Laws of 1542 prohibited new encomiendas, by which time few Indians who could be placed in encomienda remained on the islands.

hechos/matanza-de-jaragua/resumen.texto: In 1503 Ovando visited Jaragua with some 300 infantry and 70 horsemen and was welcomed with festivities by Anacaona; at a signal, his men locked the assembled caciques in a bohío and set it on fire. Las Casas, who learned of it from witnesses, speaks of some eighty caciques burned and many others killed. Anacaona was later hanged in Santo Domingo. Oviedo and Ovando's supporters justified it by a conspiracy of the caciques that no other document confirms.

hechos/guerras-de-higuey/resumen.texto: Spanish campaigns against the chiefdom of eastern Hispaniola, set off in 1502 by the death of a cacique torn apart by a Spanish dog on Saona Island and by the Taíno response, which killed several settlers. The troops of Juan de Esquivel and Juan Ponce de León took towns, killed and enslaved their inhabitants and captured Cotubanamá, who was hanged in Santo Domingo; Las Casas, who was on the island, describes the war as a hunt.

hechos/traslado-de-los-lucayos/resumen.texto: Faced with a labor shortage in Hispaniola, Ferdinand II of Aragon authorized in 1509 bringing Indians from the Bahamas, considered “useless islands” because they had no gold. Expeditions organized by Hispaniola's settlers captured them by deception and force and sold them as naborías; many ended up diving for pearls in Cubagua. By around 1520 the Bahamas were depopulated.

hechos/armadas-de-esclavos-indios/titulo.texto: Slaving Expeditions to Other Islands and to the Mainland

hechos/armadas-de-esclavos-indios/resume.texto: With licenses to capture “caribs” or Indians taken in a “just war,” expeditions from Hispaniola and Puerto Rico attacked the Lesser Antilles, the coasts of Venezuela, Florida, the Gulf of Honduras and other regions, and brought back thousands of enslaved people branded with iron. In 1520 the judge Rodrigo de Figueroa declared which islands belonged to the caribs and which to Indians who could not be enslaved; the Dominicans denounced that the expeditions provoked wars, such as the one that destroyed their mission at Cumaná in 1520.

hechos/sermon-de-montesinos-1511/resumen.texto: On the fourth Sunday of Advent 1511 the Dominican Antonio de Montesinos preached in Santo Domingo, on behalf of his entire community, led by Pedro de Córdoba, that the encomenderos were in mortal sin for the cruelty with which they treated the Indians, and asked: “Are these not men?” The settlers and Diego Columbus protested to the king, who convened the junta of theologians and jurists at Burgos, from which came the laws of 1512. The text of the sermon is known through Las Casas's History of the Indies.

hechos/repartimiento-de-1514/resumen.texto: General distribution of the Indians of Hispaniola carried out in 1514 by Rodrigo de Alburquerque and Pedro Ibáñez de Ibarra on the orders of Ferdinand II of Aragon, which redistributed some 26,000 people among settlers, officials and courtiers living in Castile. It benefited the treasurer Miguel de Pasamonte and the king's officials against Diego Columbus, and shows that in twenty years the registered Indigenous population had fallen to a fraction of its 1492 level.

hechos/renuncia-de-las-casas-a-su-encomi.texto: Bartolomé de las Casas, a cleric who had received Indians in encomienda in Cuba, recounts that while preparing a sermon he read chapter 34 of Ecclesiasticus and became convinced that everything done to the Indians was unjust. In August 1514 he announced in Sancti Spíritus that he was renouncing his Indians, and the following year he traveled to Spain to seek their freedom, the start of his half-century campaign.

hechos/gobierno-de-los-jeronimos/resumen.texto: Cardinal Cisneros, with a plan inspired by Las Casas, sent three Hieronymite friars in 1516 to govern Hispaniola with instructions to gather the Indians into free towns. The Hieronymites questioned the settlers, who denied that the Indians could live on their own; they took the Indians away from absent encomenderos but kept the encomienda, and only in 1518 began gathering the Indians into towns, when smallpox arrived. They also requested a license to bring African slaves.

hechos/epidemia-de-viruela-de-1518/resum.texto: The first smallpox epidemic documented in the Americas. The Hieronymites wrote in January 1519 that since December almost a third of the Indians of Hispaniola had died; the disease spread to Puerto Rico and Cuba and from there reached Mexico with Narváez's expedition in 1520. Earlier epidemics, such as the one that affected Spaniards and Taíno when La Isabela was founded, have not been identified with certainty; Francisco Guerra proposed that the one of 1493–1494 was an influenza of swine origin.

hechos/despoblacion-de-la-espanola/titul.texto: The Collapse of the Taíno Population of Hispaniola

hechos/despoblacion-de-la-espanola/resum.texto: Spanish counts record some 60,000 Indians in 1508, about 26,000 in 1514 and a few thousand after the smallpox of 1518; in 1542 Las Casas wrote that about two hundred remained, although by then many descendants lived mixed with Spaniards and Africans or outside the records. For 1492 estimates range from tens of thousands (ancient DNA, Fernandes and others) and around 100,000 (Rosenblat) to 200,000–300,000 (Livi-Bacci), more than three million (Las Casas) and around eight million (Cook and Borah). The documents point to war and massacres, forced labor in the mines, hunger, the separation of families and the fall in births, flight and suicide as causes, and from 1518 epidemics; Livi-Bacci gives more weight to labor and social disruption, and others to disease. Some authors, such as David Stannard, consider it a genocide, while others dispute this because of the lack of an intent to exterminate.

hechos/rebelion-de-enriquillo/resumen.texto: Around 1519 the cacique Enriquillo rose up with his people in the Bahoruco mountains and for fourteen years defeated or evaded the expeditions sent against him, while fugitive Indians from the encomiendas joined him. In 1533 Captain Francisco de Barrionuevo, sent by Charles V, agreed with him a pardon, freedom for his people and lands in Boyá; in return Enriquillo undertook to return fugitive African slaves. Las Casas visited him that year to confirm the peace.

hechos/rebelion-de-esclavos-de-1521/resu.texto: On December 26, 1521, a group of Wolof slaves from Diego Columbus's sugar mill, near the Nigua River, rose up, joined enslaved people from other estates, killed several Spaniards and marched toward Azua. They were defeated within a few days by horsemen sent by Diego Columbus, and their leaders were hanged. It is the first major African slave rebellion documented in the Americas, and in January 1522 the island's authorities issued ordinances to control Black slaves, among the first of their kind on the continent.

hechos/azucar-y-trata-africana-en-la-esp.texto: The First Sugar Mills and the African Slave Trade in the Antilles

From 1501 the Crown allowed African slaves born in Castile to be taken to Hispaniola; Ovando asked for this to be suspended in 1503 because they fled with the Indians. When gold ran out, settlers set up sugar mills from around 1516, and in 1518 Charles I granted Laurent de Gouvenot a license to bring 4,000 enslaved people directly from Africa, the first major slave-trade license to the Americas. In 1516 Las Casas had proposed bringing Africans to relieve the Indians, and years later he wrote that he regretted it, because the enslavement of Black people was as unjust as that of the Indians.

hechos/cimarrones-de-la-espanola/resumen.texto: From the 1520s fugitive African slaves formed groups in the mountains of Hispaniola that attacked sugar mills and roads, sometimes together with Indians. Letters from the Audiencia mention leaders such as Diego de Guzmán and Sebastián Lemba, who died in 1547; the authorities organized squads and paid rewards for fugitives.

hechos/fundacion-de-santo-domingo/resume.texto: Bartolomé Columbus founded the town on the eastern bank of the Ozama around 1496–1498, near the gold mines of San Cristóbal, and the population of La Isabela moved there. After the hurricane of 1502 Ovando rebuilt it on the western bank with streets laid out in a grid, one of the first regular layouts in the Americas.

hechos/fundacion-del-hospital-san-nicola.texto: Founding of the Hospital of San Nicolás de Bari
Hospital of San Nicolás de Bari

Nicolás de Ovando founded around 1503 in Santo Domingo a hospital for the poor and sick, later sustained by a confraternity, considered the first in the Americas. The stone building, with three naves, was built in the following decades; the exact date of the founding is not documented with precision.

hechos/audiencia-de-santo-domingo/resume.texto: Court of appeal created in 1511, the first in the Americas, which limited the judicial powers of Viceroy Diego Columbus and was definitively organized in 1526. Its jurisdiction covered the Antilles, Venezuela and Florida; after the cession of Santo Domingo to France it moved to Puerto Príncipe, in Cuba, in 1799–1800.

hechos/construccion-de-la-catedral-de-sa.texto: Construction of the Cathedral of Santo Domingo
Cathedral of Santa María de la Encarnación

The diocese of Santo Domingo was created in 1511 and the stone cathedral was built approximately between 1521 and 1541. In 1546 Pope Paul III raised it to a metropolitan see and declared it primate of the Indies.

hechos/fundacion-de-la-universidad-de-sa.texto: Founding of the University of Santo Domingo
University of Santo Tomás de Aquino

Paul III's bull In apostolatus culmine, of October 28, 1538, raised to university status the general study that the Dominicans had had in Santo Domingo since around 1518. According to Dominican historiography it received royal approval only in 1558 and operated with interruptions; for that reason the universities of San Marcos in Lima and of Mexico, created by royal decree in 1551 and with continuous operation, also claim to be the first in the Americas. The original bull is not preserved.

hechos/conquista-de-puerto-rico/resumen.texto: Juan Ponce de León, received in 1508 by the cacique Agüeybaná, founded Caparra, and from 1509 the settlers distributed the Taíno among themselves in encomienda to wash gold. In 1511 the caciques rose up and killed the encomendero Cristóbal de Sotomayor and other settlers; Oviedo recounts that earlier they had drowned a Spaniard, Diego Salcedo, to see whether the Christians were mortal. The rebellion was defeated, the prisoners were enslaved and branded, and for years fugitive Taíno and Caribs attacked the island from the Lesser Antilles.

hechos/conquista-de-jamaica/resumen.texto: Juan de Esquivel occupied Jamaica in 1509 on the orders of Diego Columbus and founded Sevilla la Nueva; the island, which had no gold, supplied casabe, cotton and livestock to the expeditions to the mainland. The island's Taíno disappeared from the records within a few decades, and the capital moved in 1534 to the Villa de la Vega; from 1536 Jamaica was a hereditary marquisate of the Columbus family.

hechos/conquista-de-cuba/resumen.texto: Diego Velázquez landed in eastern Cuba around 1510–1511 with some 300 men, overcame the resistance of Hatuey and founded Baracoa; Pánfilo de Narváez then toured the island westward with Las Casas as chaplain. Between 1511 and 1515 seven towns were founded, from Baracoa and Bayamo to Havana and Santiago, and the Taíno were distributed in encomienda for the gold mines. Las Casas, a witness to the campaign, described it as a succession of abuses, the gravest episode of which was Caonao.

hechos/ejecucion-de-hatuey/resumen.texto: The cacique Hatuey, captured after months of resistance in eastern Cuba, was burned alive near Yara in early 1512 on the orders of Diego Velázquez. Las Casas recounts in A Short Account of the Destruction of the Indies that a friar offered him baptism so that he could go to heaven, and that he refused on learning that there were also Christians there; the account, which Las Casas did not witness, turned Hatuey into the first symbol of Indigenous resistance in Cuba.

hechos/matanza-de-caonao/resumen.texto: In the Taíno village of Caonao, in central Cuba, soldiers of Pánfilo de Narváez, who had been received with food, suddenly attacked the inhabitants gathered there and killed men, women and children with their swords. Las Casas, who was present and tried to stop them, speaks of thousands dead; it is the only detailed source on the episode and gives no clear cause for the attack.

hechos/fundacion-de-la-habana/resumen.texto: The town of San Cristóbal de La Habana was founded in 1514 on the south coast of Cuba and around 1519 moved to the northern bay. Its port became the meeting point for the fleets returning to Spain and, after the fire set by the corsair Jacques de Sores in 1555, the most heavily fortified town in the Caribbean.

hechos/saqueo-de-santo-domingo-1586/resu.texto: In January 1586, during the Anglo-Spanish war, Francis Drake's fleet landed near Santo Domingo, occupied the city for a month, burned part of it and extracted a ransom of 25,000 ducats before continuing toward Cartagena. The attack showed the defensive weakness of the Spanish Antilles.

hechos/devastaciones-de-osorio/resumen.texto: On the orders of Philip III, Governor Antonio de Osorio depopulated the towns of northern and western Hispaniola, such as Puerto Plata, Montecristi, Bayajá and La Yaguana, to cut off the smuggling of hides with the Dutch, English and French and the circulation of Protestant Bibles. The residents and their livestock were forcibly moved near Santo Domingo, and many died; the empty west was left to feral cattle, the buccaneers and later the French colony.

hechos/colonias-de-san-cristobal/titulo.texto: English and French Colonies on Saint Kitts

hechos/colonias-de-san-cristobal/resumen.texto: Thomas Warner founded in 1624 the first stable English colony in the Antilles, and Pierre Belain d'Esnambuc set up a French one on the same island in 1625; they divided it between them. It was the base for English expansion to Nevis, Antigua and Montserrat and for French expansion to Guadeloupe and Martinique; France ceded its share to Great Britain in 1713.

hechos/matanza-de-los-kalinagos-de-1626/.texto: Massacre of the Kalinago on Saint Kitts

English and French settlers, who said they had been warned by a Kalinago woman of a plan to attack them, surprised the island's Kalinago at night and killed many, then fought at Bloody Point those who came from other islands. The figure of some 2,000 dead that is repeated comes from later accounts and is uncertain; the survivors were expelled from Saint Kitts. Part of the historiography describes it as genocide.

hechos/colonizacion-de-barbados/titulo.texto: English Colonization of Barbados and the Sugar Revolution

hechos/colonizacion-de-barbados/resumen.texto: English settlers occupied Barbados in 1627, then uninhabited, and devoted it to tobacco and cotton worked by contracted European servants. From the 1640s they adopted sugar, using techniques learned from the Dutch in Brazil, and the island came to have a majority of African slaves, governed by the code of 1661; by around 1680 there were some 38,000 enslaved people and some 20,000 whites, according to a census of the time. It was the model plantation colony of the English Antilles and of South Carolina.

hechos/plantaciones-codrington/titulo.texto: The Codrington Plantations of the Church of England

hechos/plantaciones-codrington/resumen.texto: Christopher Codrington, a planter born in Barbados and governor of the Leeward Islands, bequeathed on his death in 1710 his two sugar plantations in Barbados, with their enslaved people, to the Society for the Propagation of the Gospel, the missionary society of the Church of England, to support a college, which opened in 1745. The Society worked the plantations with slave labor until British abolition (1834–1838), and in its first decades branded enslaved people with the word “Society.” In 2006 the General Synod of the Church of England asked forgiveness for the Church's participation in slavery, and this case was recalled in the debate.

hechos/mito-de-los-esclavos-irlandeses/r.texto: In the 17th century thousands of Irish, Scots and English went to Barbados and other islands as indentured servants or as prisoners deported by Cromwell, with harsh work and punishments but for a limited time and without their status passing to their children. Since the late 20th century, and especially on the internet, the claim has circulated that they were “slaves” equal to or worse off than Africans, often to minimize African slavery. Historians such as Liam Hogan have shown that it confuses temporary servitude with hereditary slavery and uses false images and figures.

hechos/colonias-francesas-de-las-antilla.texto: French Colonies of Guadeloupe and Martinique

The Company of the Isles of America, created by Richelieu in 1635, occupied Guadeloupe and Martinique with settlers and contracted servants (“engagés”). There were wars with the Kalinago, who were expelled from Martinique in 1658, and from the middle of the century the islands turned to sugar with African slaves; in 1674 the Crown took over direct government.

hechos/paz-de-1660-con-los-caribes/resum.texto: Agreement signed in Basse-Terre by French and English governors and Kalinago chiefs, which reserved Dominica and Saint Vincent for the Kalinago in exchange for leaving the other islands. It ended a period of wars, but the reserved islands were occupied by the British after 1763.

hechos/conquista-inglesa-de-jamaica/resu.texto: The expedition sent by Oliver Cromwell under William Penn and Robert Venables, which had failed before Santo Domingo in April 1655, took Jamaica in May. Spaniards and the enslaved people freed by them resisted in the mountains until 1660, when Juan de Bolas's palenque went over to the English; Spain recognized the possession in the Treaty of Madrid of 1670. The former slaves who remained free in the mountains were the origin of the Jamaican Maroons.

hechos/bucaneros-y-filibusteros/resumen.texto: The buccaneers were hunters of feral cattle in western Hispaniola who smoked the meat in “boucans”; based at Tortuga and later at Port Royal, many became filibusters who attacked Spanish ships and ports with letters of marque from the governors. The campaigns of L'Olonnais and Morgan sacked Maracaibo, Portobelo and Panama; their era ended when England and France, after the Treaty of Ryswick of 1697, began to pursue them.

hechos/terremoto-de-port-royal/resumen.texto: On June 7, 1692, an earthquake sank about two-thirds of Port Royal, the port of the buccaneers and of Jamaica's slave trade, into the sea; some 2,000 people died immediately and thousands more from their injuries and the diseases that followed. Preachers presented it as divine punishment, and the commercial capital moved to Kingston.

hechos/colonia-de-saint-domingue/resumen.texto: Western Hispaniola, occupied by French buccaneers, came de facto under French control after the Treaty of Ryswick (1697), and its border was fixed in the Treaty of Aranjuez (1777). In 1789 it was the world's largest producer of sugar and coffee, with around half a million enslaved people, some 30,000 whites and some 28,000 free people of color, according to the censuses of the time. Mortality was so high that the enslaved population was sustained only by the arrival of tens of thousands of Africans each year.

hechos/curazao-holandesa/titulo.texto: Dutch Curaçao and the Slave Trade

hechos/curazao-holandesa/resumen.texto: The Dutch West India Company took Curaçao from Spain in 1634 and from the 1660s turned it into a depot for African slaves who were resold to Spanish America, legally under asientos or through smuggling. Its population included a Jewish community of Sephardic origin that arrived from Amsterdam and Brazil, and a creole language, Papiamento.

hechos/rebelion-de-curazao-1795/resumen.texto: In August 1795 enslaved people from the Knip plantation on Curaçao, led by Tula, rose up invoking the Haitian revolution and the French occupation of the Netherlands, which in their view should bring them freedom. After a month of fighting they were defeated; Tula was tortured and executed in October along with other leaders.

hechos/indias-occidentales-danesas/resum.texto: The Danish West India Company occupied Saint Thomas in 1672 and Saint John in 1718 and bought Saint Croix from France in 1733, islands devoted to sugar and the slave trade. Denmark was the first European state to prohibit the Atlantic slave trade, by a decree of 1792 that took effect in 1803; slavery was abolished in July 1848, when Governor Peter von Scholten declared it in the face of a rebellion on Saint Croix.

hechos/mision-morava-de-santo-tomas/titu.texto: Moravian Mission among the Enslaved People of the Danish West Indies

hechos/mision-morava-de-santo-tomas/resu.texto: In December 1732 Leonhard Dober and David Nitschmann, the first missionaries of the Moravian Brethren, sent by Count Zinzendorf to preach to African slaves, arrived in Saint Thomas, in one of the first Protestant missions directed at them. Many planters opposed them because they feared that baptized and literate enslaved people would demand freedom, and some missionaries were imprisoned; the Moravians, by contrast, did not question slavery, and Zinzendorf, visiting in 1739, urged the enslaved to obey their masters. The mission formed congregations of enslaved people on the three Danish islands and from there spread to other Caribbean colonies.

hechos/rebelion-de-san-juan-1733/titulo.texto: Enslaved People's Rebellion on Saint John

hechos/rebelion-de-san-juan-1733/resumen.texto: In November 1733, months after a very harsh code of punishments issued by Governor Philip Gardelin, enslaved people of Akwamu origin took the fort at Coral Bay and controlled most of the Danish island of Saint John for about six months. They were defeated in 1734 with French troops brought from Martinique, and many of the rebels took their own lives before surrendering.

hechos/primera-guerra-cimarrona/resumen.texto: War between the British government of Jamaica and the communities of enslaved people who had escaped to the mountains: the Windward Maroons, associated with Nanny and Quao, and the Leeward Maroons, led by Cudjoe. The British took Nanny Town in 1734 but failed to defeat them, and in 1739 they signed treaties recognizing the Maroons' freedom and lands in exchange for returning fugitives and helping against revolts.

hechos/rebelion-de-tacky/resumen.texto: Uprising of enslaved people of Akan origin (“coromantee”) that began in April 1760 in the parish of Saint Mary, in Jamaica, led by Tacky, and spread to the west of the island. The British suppressed it with help from the Maroons, one of whom killed Tacky; some 60 whites and hundreds of rebels died, and many were executed by burning at the stake or in cages. Edward Long, a planter who lived on the island, narrated it in his History of Jamaica (1774) from the point of view of the slave owners.

hechos/toma-de-la-habana-1762/lugar.texto: Morro Castle (Castillo de los Tres Reyes del Morro)

hechos/toma-de-la-habana-1762/resumen.texto: During the Seven Years' War a British expedition under the Earl of Albemarle besieged Havana from June 1762; El Morro fell on July 30 in the assault in which its defender, Luis Vicente de Velasco, was mortally wounded, and the city surrendered in August. During the occupation the British opened the port to trade and sold thousands of enslaved people; in 1763 they returned Havana in exchange for Florida, and Spain then strengthened the defenses and reformed Cuba's trade.

hechos/fundacion-de-la-universidad-de-la.texto: Founding of the University of Havana

In 1721 the Dominicans obtained a bull from Innocent XIII and later royal approval to found a university in their convent in Havana, which opened on January 5, 1728, as the Royal and Pontifical University of San Jerónimo. It taught theology, law, medicine and the arts, and was secularized in 1842.

hechos/guerras-caribes-de-san-vicente/re.texto: Great Britain received Saint Vincent in 1763, and its plans to sell the lands of the Black Caribs led to the first war (1772–1773), which ended with a treaty leaving them part of the island. In 1795, with support from the French of Victor Hugues, the Garifuna led by Joseph Chatoyer rose again; Chatoyer died in March of that year and the resistance surrendered in 1796.

hechos/deportacion-de-los-garifunas/resu.texto: The Garifuna, or Black Caribs, of Saint Vincent descended from Kalinago and from Africans who had arrived as castaways or fugitives in the 17th century, and they spoke the language of the Kalinago. After their defeat in 1796 the British confined some 4,000 or 5,000 to the islet of Balliceaux, where nearly half died of disease, and in April 1797 landed some 2,000 or 2,500 on Roatán, off Honduras. From there they spread along the coasts of Honduras, Belize, Guatemala and Nicaragua, where their descendants live.

hechos/cesion-de-santo-domingo-a-francia.texto: Cession of Santo Domingo to France

Under the Treaty of Basel of 1795 Spain ceded its part of Hispaniola to France. Toussaint Louverture occupied it in January 1801 and abolished slavery there; many Spanish families emigrated to Cuba, Puerto Rico and Venezuela, and the university ceased to function. The creoles of Santo Domingo, with British help, returned the colony to Spain in 1809.

hechos/proceso-de-mackandal/resumen.texto: In 1757–1758 the authorities of Saint-Domingue attributed a wave of deaths of settlers, enslaved people and animals to a network of poisoners led by the Maroon François Mackandal, who was captured and burned alive in Cap-Français in January 1758. Trials and executions of other enslaved people accused of poisoning followed. Historians debate whether there was an organized conspiracy or whether the settlers' panic attributed to poison deaths that were caused by disease.

hechos/rebelion-de-oge/resumen.texto: In October 1790 Vincent Ogé and Jean-Baptiste Chavannes rose up in northern Saint-Domingue with a few hundred free people of color to demand that the equal political rights they believed had been recognized in Paris be applied. Defeated, they fled to the Spanish part, which handed them over; in February 1791 they were broken on the wheel in Cap-Français, which radicalized the free people of color and led the French National Assembly to recognize the rights of some of them in May.

hechos/ceremonia-de-bois-caiman/resumen.texto: Interrogations of 1791 document a meeting of enslaved leaders from the Northern plantations on August 14 to prepare the uprising. The religious ceremony in a forest, with a priestess, the sacrifice of a pig and an oath led by Boukman, first appears in the account of the settler Antoine Dalmas, published in 1814, and was expanded by 19th-century Haitian historians. David Geggus concludes that there probably was a ceremony but that its details are uncertain, and Léon-François Hoffmann considered it largely a national myth; the idea, spread by some evangelical preachers, that it was a “pact with the devil” has no documentary basis.

hechos/levantamiento-de-1791/titulo.texto: Uprising of Enslaved People in Northern Saint-Domingue

hechos/levantamiento-de-1791/resumen.texto: On the night of August 22–23, 1791, enslaved people of the Northern Plain rose up under leaders such as Boukman, Jean-François and Biassou; within about two months they set fire to hundreds of plantations and killed about 2,000 whites, according to the settlers' estimates. The settlers responded with mass executions of prisoners. It was the beginning of the Haitian revolution and the largest slave rebellion in the history of the Americas.

hechos/revolucion-haitiana/resumen.texto: A process that began with the conflict between white settlers and free people of color after the French Revolution and with the 1791 uprising of enslaved people, continued with abolition in 1793–1794, the rise of Toussaint Louverture and the wars against the British and Spanish, and ended with the defeat of Napoleon's expedition and Haiti's independence in 1804. All sides committed documented massacres of prisoners and civilians, and war and epidemics caused hundreds of thousands of deaths according to most estimates. C. L. R. James read it as a slave revolution within the French Revolution, and recent historiography (Geggus, Dubois) stresses its Atlantic dimension; in the 19th century slaveholders in the United States, Cuba and Brazil invoked it as a warning, and abolitionists as proof of the enslaved people's capacity to free themselves.

hechos/abolicion-de-la-esclavitud-en-sai.texto: Commissioner Sonthonax proclaimed the freedom of enslaved people in the North on August 29, 1793, and his colleague Polverel extended it to the West and South; the National Convention ratified it and extended it to all colonies on February 4, 1794. The former slaves were required by regulations to keep working on the plantations in exchange for a share of the harvest; in May 1794 Toussaint Louverture left the Spanish side and went over to the French.

hechos/ocupacion-britanica-de-saint-domi.texto: Invited by settlers who wished to preserve slavery, British troops occupied ports in the west and south of Saint-Domingue from 1793, including Port-au-Prince. Yellow fever and the war against Toussaint's forces caused thousands of deaths among the British, who in 1798 negotiated their withdrawal with him.

hechos/guerra-del-sur/resumen.texto: War between Toussaint Louverture, who dominated the north and west, and the free man of color general André Rigaud, who controlled the south. Toussaint won and Rigaud went into exile; Dessalines's repression of Rigaud's supporters, many of them free people of color, caused thousands of deaths according to contemporary testimonies, whose figures are disputed.

hechos/expedicion-de-leclerc/resumen.texto: At the end of 1801 Napoleon sent his brother-in-law Leclerc, who landed in February 1802 with tens of thousands of soldiers to restore French authority; after months of fighting, Toussaint surrendered and was then captured and deported. When it became known that France was restoring slavery in Guadeloupe, the former slaves and their generals rose again; yellow fever killed Leclerc and most of the soldiers, and his successor Rochambeau responded with mass drownings, executions and attack dogs. France lost the colony in November 1803.

hechos/batalla-de-vertieres/resumen.texto: On November 18, 1803, Dessalines's army, with generals such as François Capois, took the fort of Vertières, on the outskirts of Cap-Français. Rochambeau capitulated the next day and evacuated the city, surrendering to the British fleet blockading the coast.

hechos/independencia-de-haiti/resumen.texto: On January 1, 1804, Dessalines and his generals proclaimed independence in Gonaïves, using the Indigenous name Haiti: it was the second independent state in the Americas and the first founded by former slaves. The powers were slow to recognize it; France did so in 1825 in exchange for an indemnity of 150 million francs, later reduced to 90, which Haiti paid for decades with loans, and the United States in 1862.

hechos/matanza-de-los-franceses-de-1804/.texto: Massacre of the French in Haiti

Between February and April 1804, on Dessalines's orders, Haitian soldiers killed most of the French who remained in the towns, men, women and children; estimates range from 3,000 to 5,000 dead, and some reach 7,000. A few doctors, priests and artisans were spared, as were women married to Haitians and the Polish and German soldiers who had defected to the Haitian side. Dessalines presented it as revenge for French crimes and as a defense against a reconquest; Philippe Girard and other authors analyze it as a genocide, and others as the continuation of the “war of extermination” that the two sides waged on each other in 1802–1803.

hechos/nombre-de-america/resumen.texto: Matthias Ringmann and Martin Waldseemüller proposed at Saint-Dié in 1507 calling the new southern lands “America” in honor of Amerigo Vespucci, to whom the letter to Soderini attributed their discovery. Waldseemüller dropped the name in 1516, but Mercator applied it in 1538 to the entire continent, and it became established in Europe, while Spain continued officially using “las Indias.” Las Casas accused Vespucci of taking away Columbus's glory; the theories that the name comes from the Amerrisque range in Nicaragua or from the Bristol merchant Richard Amerike lack documentary support.

hechos/mito-de-la-tierra-plana/titulo.texto: The Myth That Columbus Proved the Earth Was Round

hechos/mito-de-la-tierra-plana/resumen.texto: European scholars had known since antiquity that the Earth was spherical, as medieval university textbooks taught; the objection of the experts who examined Columbus's project between 1486 and 1491 concerned the size of the ocean, and they were right: Columbus calculated a distance to Asia far shorter than the real one. The idea that they rejected it because they believed in a flat Earth was spread by Washington Irving's novelized biography (1828) and by 19th-century textbooks. Jeffrey Burton Russell studied the origin of the myth in Inventing the Flat Earth (1991).

hechos/batalla-de-croix-des-bouquets/res.texto: On 22 March 1792, the free men of color of Beauvais and Rigaud, expelled from Port-au-Prince and reinforced by enslaved insurgents from the Cul-de-Sac plain under Yacinthe, repulsed at Croix-des-Bouquets the national guard and line detachments of the white colonists, who withdrew in disorder. According to Schœlcher, who relies on Madiou and Lacroix, the whites lost more than a hundred men, and the insurgents, armed mostly with knives, pikes and hoes, numbered about 1,200.

hechos/batalla-de-cap-francais-1793/resu.texto: On 20 June 1793 General Galbaud, removed from the colony's government by the civil commissioners Sonthonax and Polverel, landed with sailors and white colonists against the commissioners and the free people of color. After two days of street fighting, the commissioners offered freedom to the enslaved rebels who fought for the Republic, and some ten thousand of them, under Macaya and Pierrot, entered the city on 21 June; Cap-Français was looted and burned until the 26th, civilians were killed according to witnesses, and most of the white population embarked with Galbaud on the 24th.

hechos/batalla-de-crete-a-pierrot/resume.texto: Between 2 or 4 and 24 March 1802, depending on the source, the garrison of Crête-à-Pierrot, under Lamartinière, withstood the siege by Leclerc's forces and three French assaults (the first starting on the 4th, the one of the 11th or 12th in which General Dugua fell, and the one of the 22nd), while Dessalines and Toussaint attacked the besiegers from outside; on the night of the 24th it broke the encirclement on Dessalines's orders. French losses are counted in the hundreds or thousands, depending on the source. According to the French account, inside the fort there were «many whites murdered», and at Verrettes some 800 colonists had their throats slit; Rochambeau had some 600 wounded prisoners executed. Christophe's surrender was followed by Dessalines's and then Toussaint's, in May.

hechos/virreinato-colombino/titulo.texto: The Columbian viceroyalty and the Columbian lawsuits

hechos/virreinato-colombino/resumen.texto: The Capitulations of Santa Fe (17 April 1492) gave Columbus and his heirs the titles of admiral of the Ocean Sea and viceroy and governor-general of the lands he would discover, with economic prerogatives; Columbus governed Hispaniola with his brothers as deputies until Bobadilla's investigation had him arrested in 1500. His son Diego, after bringing the Columbian lawsuits against the crown, obtained in 1511 recognition of a viceroyalty limited to what his father had discovered; the 1536 settlement with his heir Luis, who received the dukedom of Veragua and the marquisate of Jamaica, ended the viceroyalty.

hechos/capitania-general-de-santo-doming.texto: Political and military jurisdiction over Hispaniola and, originally, over much of the Caribbean, under the Audiencia of Santo Domingo. Accounts date its origin differently: to 1492, with the first colonization, or to 1535, when the viceroyalty of New Spain was created; from May 1577 the president of the Audiencia was also governor and captain general. Spain ceded the western third of the island to France in 1697 and the rest in 1795; France occupied it between 1801 and 1809, and the Creoles declared independence in 1821.

hechos/segunda-guerra-cimarrona/resumen.texto: Eight months of guerrilla war between the Maroons of Trelawny Town and the British government of Jamaica, sparked by the whipping of two Maroons accused of stealing pigs and by the arrest, on the orders of Governor Balcarres, of six delegates who were going to present complaints. The British, with some 5,000 soldiers and militiamen, suffered more casualties than the Maroons, but General Walpole's scorched-earth campaign and the use of dogs brought from Cuba led the Maroons to sign with Walpole, in December 1795, a treaty promising to resettle them within the island. As most did not surrender until mid-March 1796, after the 1 January deadline set by the governor, he deemed the treaty broken and deported some 581 of them to Nova Scotia. Those of Accompong fought alongside the British, and those of Windward remained neutral.

lugares/banwari-trace/resumen.texto: Shell midden in southern Trinidad, one of the oldest archaeological sites in the insular Caribbean, occupied by Archaic hunters, fishers and gatherers about 7,000 years ago. A human skeleton, one of the oldest in the region, was found there in 1969.

lugares/tibes/resumen.texto: Site near Ponce, in Puerto Rico, with plazas and ballcourts (bateyes) bounded by stones and a cemetery, used by Saladoid and Ostionoid populations before the height of the Taíno. It was discovered in 1975 and is one of the oldest ceremonial centers in the Antilles.

lugares/caguana/resumen.texto: Complex of ballcourts and plazas from the Taíno period in Utuado, in central Puerto Rico, with carved monoliths bearing petroglyphs of human figures and beings from mythology. It was excavated by John Alden Mason in 1915 and is one of the largest pre-Columbian ceremonial sites in the Antilles; its ballcourts date to around 1270.

lugares/la-navidad/resumen.texto: Fort that Columbus built with the remains of the Santa María on the north coast of present-day Haiti, where he left 39 men in January 1493. On returning in November he found it destroyed and without survivors; its exact location is unknown, and Kathleen Deagan proposed the site of En Bas Saline, which she identified as the village of Guacanagarí.

lugares/la-isabela/resumen.texto: The first Spanish town in the Americas, founded by Columbus in January 1494 on the north coast of Hispaniola, with a church, the admiral's house, a storehouse and stone walls. Hunger, disease and mutinies emptied it within a few years in favor of Santo Domingo; its ruins, excavated since 1987 by José María Cruxent and Kathleen Deagan, are now an archaeological park.

lugares/santo-domingo/resumen.texto: City founded by Bartolomé Columbus on the eastern bank of the Ozama River around 1496–1498 and moved by Ovando to the western bank after the hurricane of 1502, laid out on a grid. It was the capital of the Indies in the first decades: seat of the first audiencia, the first cathedral and the first hospital and university in the Americas; its colonial city has been a World Heritage Site since 1990.

lugares/fortaleza-ozama/resumen.texto: Stone fortress built from 1502 at the mouth of the Ozama by order of Ovando, the oldest surviving European military construction in the Americas. Gonzalo Fernández de Oviedo was its alcaide from 1533.

lugares/hospital-san-nicolas-de-bari/nom.texto: Hospital of San Nicolás de Bari

lugares/hospital-san-nicolas-de-bari/res.texto: Hospital in Santo Domingo founded by Nicolás de Ovando around 1503 for the poor and sick, the first in the Americas. The stone building was erected in the following decades; damaged by Drake in 1586 and by earthquakes, it was partly demolished in 1911, and its ruins remain today.

lugares/alcazar-de-colon/resumen.texto: Palace that Diego Columbus and his wife María de Toledo had built in Santo Domingo between 1510 and 1514 as the viceroy's residence. It is the oldest viceregal residence in the Americas; restored in the 20th century, it operates as a museum.

lugares/catedral-de-santo-domingo/nombre.texto: Cathedral of Santa María de la Encarnación

lugares/catedral-de-santo-domingo/resume.texto: Cathedral of Santo Domingo, seat of one of the first dioceses in the Americas (1511). Its stone construction, between Late Gothic and Renaissance styles, was carried out approximately between 1521 and 1541; in 1546 Paul III declared it primate of the Indies.

lugares/universidad-de-santo-tomas-de-aq.texto: University of Santo Tomás de Aquino

University created on the Dominicans' general study in Santo Domingo by the bull In apostolatus culmine of 1538. It operated with interruptions and was closed during the cession to France and the Haitian occupation at the beginning of the 19th century; the present Autonomous University of Santo Domingo is considered its heir.

lugares/caparra/resumen.texto: First Spanish settlement in Puerto Rico, founded by Juan Ponce de León in 1508 near the bay of San Juan. It was abandoned around 1519–1521, when the town moved to the islet of San Juan; the foundations of Ponce de León's house remain.

lugares/san-juan-de-puerto-rico/resumen.texto: City founded on the islet in San Juan Bay around 1519–1521, when the residents of Caparra moved there. It was the military key of the Antilles, with the fortresses of El Morro and San Cristóbal, which withstood English and Dutch attacks; the Englishman George Clifford took it briefly in 1598.

lugares/sevilla-la-nueva/resumen.texto: First Spanish town in Jamaica, founded by Juan de Esquivel in 1509 on the north coast, near the Bay of Santa Gloria where Columbus had been stranded in 1503–1504. It was abandoned in 1534 in favor of the Villa de la Vega, today Spanish Town; the site, previously a Taíno village and later a British plantation, is now a heritage park.

lugares/baracoa/resumen.texto: First Spanish town in Cuba, founded by Diego Velázquez in 1511 at the eastern tip of the island, and the colony's first capital. Hatuey resisted the Spaniards nearby.

lugares/santiago-de-cuba/resumen.texto: Town founded by Diego Velázquez in 1515 on the south coast of eastern Cuba; it was the capital of Cuba until the governorship passed de facto to Havana in the mid-16th century. Cortés's expedition set out from its port in 1518.

lugares/la-habana/resumen.texto: Town founded in 1514 on the south coast of Cuba and moved around 1519 to the northern bay. Its port was the meeting point for fleets returning to Spain, so it was fortified after the sack by the French corsair Jacques de Sores in 1555; it was the capital of Cuba and the most populous city in the Spanish Antilles.

lugares/castillo-del-morro-la-habana/nom.texto: Morro Castle (Castillo de los Tres Reyes del Morro)

lugares/castillo-del-morro-la-habana/res.texto: Fortress overlooking the entrance to Havana Bay, built between 1589 and 1630 to a design by the Italian engineer Juan Bautista Antonelli. The British took it in July 1762 after a 44-day siege in which its defender, Luis de Velasco, died.

lugares/universidad-de-la-habana/resumen.texto: University founded by the Dominicans as the Royal and Pontifical University of San Jerónimo of Havana, with a papal bull of 1721 and opening in 1728. It was secularized in 1842 and is the oldest university in Cuba.

lugares/bloody-point/resumen.texto: Site on the coast of Saint Kitts (San Cristóbal) where in 1626 English and French settlers killed Kalinago from the island and from neighboring islands. The name, meaning “bloody point,” recalls the massacre.

lugares/port-royal/resumen.texto: Jamaican port at the tip of Kingston Bay, base of privateers and buccaneers with English commissions after 1655 and one of the largest slave and plunder markets in the Caribbean. The 1692 earthquake sank two-thirds of the town into the sea.

lugares/tortuga/resumen.texto: Island off the north coast of Hispaniola that from the 1630s was a base for French, English and Dutch buccaneers and filibusters, and was contested with Spain. From 1665 Governor Bertrand d'Ogeron turned it into the starting point of French colonization of Saint-Domingue.

lugares/willemstad/resumen.texto: Capital of Curaçao, founded by the Dutch West India Company after it took the island from Spain in 1634. It was a major depot of African slaves for Spanish America and the site of one of the first Jewish communities in the Americas, with the Mikvé Israel-Emanuel synagogue (1732).

lugares/cap-francais/resumen.texto: Northern port of Saint-Domingue founded around 1670, capital of the colony until 1770 and its richest city. It was the center of the revolution of 1791–1803: it was burned in 1793 and in 1802, and the battle of Vertières was fought on its outskirts.

lugares/nanny-town/resumen.texto: Settlement of the Windward Maroons in the Blue Mountains, in eastern Jamaica, associated with Nanny. British troops took and destroyed it in 1734, during the First Maroon War.

lugares/accompong/resumen.texto: Maroon town in the mountains of western Jamaica whose lands were recognized in the 1739 treaty with the Leeward Maroons. Its residents maintain their own government and every January 6 celebrate the anniversary of their leader Cudjoe.

lugares/balliceaux/resumen.texto: Islet of the Grenadines, south of Saint Vincent, where the British confined some 4,000 or 5,000 defeated Garifuna in 1796–1797; nearly half died there of disease before the deportation to Roatán.

lugares/citadelle-laferriere/resumen.texto: Fortress on a mountaintop in northern Haiti, built between 1805 and 1820 by order of Dessalines and Henri Christophe to resist a French reconquest, with the forced labor of thousands of people. It has been a World Heritage Site since 1982, together with the Sans-Souci palace.

lugares/codrington-college/resumen.texto: Anglican college in Barbados supported by the sugar plantations that Christopher Codrington bequeathed in 1710, with their enslaved people, to the Society for the Propagation of the Gospel; it opened in 1745 and is one of the oldest Anglican theological colleges. Today it trains clergy and is affiliated with the University of the West Indies.
